text:
INTRODUCTION
The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the 
financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for 
the second  quarter of 2022 . 
This Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the second  quarter of 
2022  (“Form 10-Q”) should be read together with JPMorgan 
Chase’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended 
December 31, 2021  (“2021  Form 10-K”). Refer to the 
Glossary of terms and acronyms and line of business (“LOB”) 
metrics on pages 182-190  for definitions of terms and 
acronyms used throughout this Form 10-Q.
This Form 10-Q contains forward-looking statements within 
the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 
1995. These forward-looking statements are based on the 
current beliefs and expectations of JPMorgan Chase’s 
management, speak only as of the date of this Form 10-Q and 
are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. Refer to 
Forward-looking Statements on page 87  of this Form 10-Q 
and Part I, Item 1A, Risk Factors, on pages 9-33 of the 2021  
Form 10-K for a discussion of certain of those risks and 
uncertainties and the factors that could cause JPMorgan 
Chase’s actual results to differ materially because of those 
risks and uncertainties. There is no assurance that actual 
results will be in line with any outlook information set forth 
herein, and the Firm does not undertake to update any 
forward-looking statements.
JPMorgan Chase & Co.  (NYSE: JPM), a financial holding 
company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a 
leading financial services firm based in the United States of 
America  (“U.S.”) , with operations worldwide. JPMorgan 
Chase had $3.8 trillion  in assets and $286.1 billion  in 
stockholders’ equity as of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2. The Firm is a 
leader in investment banking, financial services for 
consumers and small businesses, commercial banking, 
financial transaction processing and asset management. 
Under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands, the Firm serves 
millions of customers  predominantly in the U.S., a nd many 
of the world’s most prominent corporate, institutional and 
government clients globally.  JPMorgan Chase’s principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, National Association (“JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A.”), a national banking association with U.S. branches in 
48 states and Washington, D.C. as of  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2. 
JPMorgan Chase’s principal non-bank subsidiary is J.P. 
Morgan Securities LLC (“J.P. Morgan Securities”), a U.S. 
broker-dealer. The bank and non-bank subsidiaries of 
JPMorgan Chase operate nationally as well as through 
overseas branches and subsidiaries, representative offices 
and subsidiary foreign banks. The Firm’s principal operating 
subsidiaries outside the U.S. are J.P. Morgan Securities plc 
and J.P. Morgan SE ( “JPMSE”), which are subsidiaries of 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and are based in the United 
Kingdom (“U.K.”) and Germany, respectively.
For management reporting purposes, the Firm’s activities 
are organized into four major reportable business 
segments, as well as a Corporate segment. The Firm’s 
consumer business segment is Consumer & Community 
Banking (“CCB”). The Firm’s wholesale business segments 
are the Corporate & Investment Bank (“CIB”), Commercial 
Banking (“CB”), and Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”). 
Refer to Note 25 of this Form 10-Q and Note 32 of 
JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 10-K for a description of the 
Firm’s business segments and the products and services 
they provide to their respective client bases.
The Firm's website is www.jpmorganchase.com. JPMorgan 
Chase makes available on its website, free of charge, annual 
reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and 
current reports on Form 8-K pursuant to Section 13(a) or 
Section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as 
soon as reasonably practicable after it electronically files or 
furnishes such material to the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (the “SEC”) at www.sec.gov. JPMorgan Chase 
makes new and important information about the Firm 
available on its website at https://
www.jpmorganchase.com, including on the Investor 
Relations section of its website at https://
www.jpmorganchase.com/ir. Information on the Firm's 
website is not incorporated by reference into this Form 10-
Q or the Firm’s other filings with the SEC.

title: Firmwide overview
heading: Firmwide overview
start_phrase:
For the second quarter of 2022 , JPMorgan Chase reported 
net income of $ 8.6 billion, down 28%, earnings per share 
of $2.76, an ROE of 13% and ROTCE of 17%.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A in the Q2 2022 Form 10‑Q, highlighting firmwide performance and key drivers versus Q2 2021 (and year-to-date), with references to non-GAAP measures and capital framework relief.
- Earnings and profitability: Net income $8.6B (−28%); EPS $2.76 (−27%); ROE 13%; ROTCE 17%; pre-provision profit down 7%.
- Revenue mix: Total net revenue $30.7B (+1%). Net interest income $15.1B (+19%); NII excluding Markets $13.7B (+26%) on higher rates and balance sheet growth. Noninterest revenue $15.6B (−12%) on lower Investment Banking fees, losses in Credit Adjustments & Other versus prior-year gain, net losses on equity investments, lower Card income, and $337M markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions; partially offset by higher CIB Markets revenue (Markets +15%).
- Expenses: Noninterest expense $18.7B (+6%) from continued investments (technology, marketing) and higher structural compensation, partly offset by lower revenue-related compensation.
- Credit costs and quality: Provision for credit losses $1.1B (vs. $2.3B benefit prior year), including a $428M allowance build (loan growth and modest macro deterioration) and $657M net charge-offs (down, driven by Card). Total allowance for credit losses $20.0B; allowance-to-loans coverage 1.69% (vs. 2.02%). Nonperforming assets $7.8B (down $2.0B YoY) on improved consumer credit and wholesale portfolio activity.
- Balance sheet trends: Average loans $1.1T (+7%) across businesses. Average deposits $2.5T (+9%) reflecting prior-year government actions and CCB account growth; deposits declined during Q2 2022 due to migration of non-operating balances to higher-yielding alternatives (CB) and increased consumer spending (CCB).
- Capital and liquidity: CET1 capital $207B; CET1 ratios 12.2% (Standardized) and 12.9% (Advanced); Tier 1 14.1%; Total capital 15.7%; SLR 5.3%. Tangible book value per share $69.53 (+1%); book value per share $86.38 (+2%). Notes inclusion of CECL capital transition relief.
- Non-GAAP measures: Calls out pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII/NIR excluding Markets, and managed-basis revenue, with references to reconciliation pages.
- Comparison basis: Metrics and commentary primarily compare Q2 2022 to Q2 2021 unless otherwise specified.
text:
Firmwide overview 
For the second  quarter of 2022 , JPMorgan Chase reported 
net income of $ 8.6 billion, down 28%, earnings per share 
of $2.76, an ROE of 13% and ROTCE of 17%.
•Total net revenue was up 1%, and reflected:
–Net interest income of $15.1 billion, up 19%. Net 
interest income excluding Markets was $13.7 billion, 
up 26%, driven by higher rates and balance sheet 
growth.
–Noninterest revenue was $15.6 billion, down 12%, 
predominantly driven by:
◦lower Investment Banking fees, a loss in Credit 
Adjustments & Other compared to a gain in the prior 
year, and net losses on equity investments in CIB◦lower Card income in CCB, and 
◦$337 million of markdowns on held-for-sale 
positions, primarily unfunded commitments, in the 
bridge financing portfolio in CIB and CB, 
partially offset by
◦higher CIB Markets revenue.
•Noninterest expense was up 6%, driven by continued 
investments in the business, including technology and 
marketing, and higher structural expense, primarily 
compensation, partially offset by lower revenue-related 
compensation.
•The provision for credit losses was $1.1 billion, driven by: 
–a net additi on of $428 million to the allowance for 
credit losses, primarily reflecting loan growth, as well 
as a modest deterioration in the Firm's macroeconomic 
forecast, and
5–$657 million of net charge-offs, down $77 million, 
driven by Card.
The prior year provision was a net benefit of $2.3 billion, 
reflecting a net reduction in the allowance for credit 
losses of $3.0 billion. 
•The total allowance for credit losses was $20.0 billion at 
June 30, 2022. The Firm had an allowance for loan losses 
to retained loans coverage ratio of 1.69%, compared 
with 2.02% in the prior year.
•The Firm’s nonperforming assets totaled $7.8 billion at 
June 30, 2022, a net decrease of $2.0 billion from the 
prior year, driven by lower nonaccrual loans, reflecting 
improved credit performance in consumer and net 
portfolio activity in wholesale.
•Firmwide average loans of $1.1 trillion were up 7%, 
driven by higher loans across the LOBs.
•Firmwide average deposits of $2.5 trillion were up 9%, 
reflecting the residual impact associated with 
government actions in the prior year. In CCB, the increase 
was also driven by growth from new and existing 
accounts across both consumer and small business 
customers. However, during the second quarter of 2022, 
there was a decline in deposits, including in CB due to 
migration of non-operating deposits into higher-yielding 
alternatives, and in CCB as consumer spending continued 
to grow.Selected capital-related metrics
•The Firm’s CET1 capital was $207 billion , and the 
Standardized and Advanced CET1 ratios were 12.2%  and 
12.9% , respectively.
•The Firm’s SLR was 5.3% .
•The Firm grew TBVPS, ending the second  quarter of 2022  
at $69.53 , up 1% versus the prior year.
Pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII and NIR 
excluding Markets, and total net revenue on a managed 
basis are non-GAAP financial measures. Refer to 
Explanation and Reconciliation of the Firm’s Use of Non-
GAAP Financial Measures on pages 18-19  for a further 
discussion of each of these measures.

summary:

- War in Ukraine:
  - The firm has closed positions and reduced exposures related to the conflict, helping clients manage or exit pre-existing obligations and Russia-related risks.
  - Exposure to Russia and Russia-associated clients/counterparties is not material to the firm’s financial condition or results.
  - Secondary effects—market volatility, inflationary pressures, and sanctions—could adversely affect businesses.
  - Ongoing monitoring of operational risks, including sanctions compliance and heightened cyber risk.
  - Defines “Russia” and “Russia-associated” based on internal country risk criteria and sanctions associations.
  - Points to other sections (credit, market, country, and operational risk) for detailed information.

  - Continued progress transitioning from LIBOR and other IBORs to transaction-based benchmark rates in line with IOSCO standards.

  - References prior disclosures for additional background.
text:
War in Ukraine
The duration and potential outcomes of the war in Ukraine 
remain uncertain. The Firm has taken steps to close 
positions and reduce exposures connected with the war, 
and continues to assist clients with fulfilling or terminating 
pre-existing obligations and managing their Russia-related 
risks.
The Firm’s exposure to Russia and Russia-associated clients 
and counterparties is not material to its financial condition 
or results of operations. However, the secondary impacts of 
the war in Ukraine, including increased market volatility, 
inflationary pressures and the effects of financial and 
economic sanctions imposed by various governments, could 
have adverse effects on the Firm’s businesses.
The Firm also continues to monitor and manage the 
operational risks associated with the war, including 
compliance with the financial and economic sanctions and 
the increased risk of cyber attacks.
Refer to Wholesale Credit Portfolio on pages 62-70, 
Allowance for Credit Losses on pages 71-73, Market Risk 
Management on pages 75-79 , Country Risk Management on 
pages 80-81  and Operational Risk Management on page 82 
for additional information.
For purposes of this Form 10-Q, “Russia” refers to exposure 
to clients and counterparties of the Firm for which the 
largest proportion of their assets is located, or the largest 
proportion of their revenue is derived, in Russia, based on 
the Firm’s internal country risk management framework; 
and “Russia-associated” refers to exposure to clients and 
counterparties of the Firm with respect to which economic 
or financial sanctions relating to the war in Ukraine have 
been imposed or which have close association with Russia.

text:
JPMorgan Chase and other market participants continue to 
make progress with respect to the transition from the use of 
the London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) and other 
IBORs to comply with the International Organization of 
Securities Commission's standards for transaction-based 
benchmark rates. The cessation of the publication of the 
principal tenors of the U.S. dollar LIBOR (i.e., overnight, 
one-month, three-month, six-month and 12-month LIBOR) 
is scheduled for June 30, 2023.
The Firm continues its client outreach with respect to U.S. 
dollar LIBOR-linked loans and continues to monitor and 
evaluate client, industry, market, regulatory and legislative 
developments. Refer to Business Developments on pages 
50-51 of JPMorgan Chase's 2021 Form 10-K for additional 
information.

- Principal transactions: Q2 increased, led by strong Fixed Income Markets (macro, especially Currencies & EM) and Equity Markets (derivatives), but partially offset by:
  - Q2: $218MM loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (vs. $233MM gain prior year) and $337MM markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (CIB and CB); Corporate saw net gains on legacy private equity vs. prior-year losses.
  - YTD: Down overall due to a $742MM loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (funding spread widening, and losses tied to commodities and Russia-related exposures), the $337MM bridge markdowns, and Corporate private equity losses vs. prior-year gains; partially offset by stronger Markets (Fixed Income macro and Equity prime brokerage/derivatives).
  - Note: CIB Markets performance assessed on total revenue; principal transactions may offset with NII.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Increased (Q2 and YTD), driven by higher deposit-related fees in CCB and higher cash management fees in CIB and CB (YTD).

title: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
heading: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
summary:
- Scope: Analysis of significant changes in consolidated balance sheets (assets, liabilities, and equity) between December 31, 2021 and June 30, 2022, plus drivers behind those changes.
- Total size: Total assets up 3% to $3.84T; total liabilities up 3% to $3.56T; stockholders’ equity down 3% to $286B.

Assets
- Cash and deposits: Cash and due from banks slightly up; deposits with banks down 10% due to Markets activities and loan growth; central bank placements noted.
- Securities financing: Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements up 23%; securities borrowed down 2%; increases driven by Markets activity, higher collateral needs, demand to cover shorts, and netting effects.
- Trading assets: Up 7% on higher FX and commodity derivative receivables and higher debt instruments, partly offset by lower equities; additional deployment in Treasury and CIO.
- Investment securities: Portfolio reshaping with $73.2B transferred from AFS to HTM; AFS down 28% (paydowns, unrealized losses in AOCI, partly offset by net purchases); HTM up 21% (purchases partly offset by paydowns); total investment securities roughly flat.
- Loans: Up 2% driven by higher revolver use and originations in Commercial Banking, higher retained residential real estate in AWM and Home Lending, higher Card balances from consumer spending, and higher wholesale loans in CIB; partially offset by lower mortgage warehouse loans and PPP forgiveness in CBB.
- Allowance for loan losses: Up 8% (net addition of $1.4B) due to heavier weighting of adverse scenarios tied to inflation, monetary policy shifts, geopolitical risks (including war in Ukraine), modest macro deterioration, loan growth (Card, CB), and Russia-related downgrades (CIB, AWM).
- Accrued interest and receivables: Up 42% from higher client receivables tied to Markets (including prime brokerage).
- Goodwill, MSRs, and intangibles: Up 5% on MSR valuation increases (rate-driven) and acquisitions (Frosch Travel Group in CCB; Volkswagen Payments S.A. in CIB).
- Other assets: Up 10% from higher cash collateral placed with counterparties and increased securities financing in Markets.

Liabilities and equity
- Deposits: Flat overall; growth from new CCB accounts and higher balances in Securities Services and Payments offset by declines in CB (migration to higher-yielding alternatives) and seasonality in AWM and CB.
- Securities financing liabilities: Federal funds purchased and securities loaned/sold under repos up 15% on higher secured financing of trading assets and netting in Markets, partly offset by lower secured financing of AFS in Treasury and CIO.
- Short-term borrowings: Up 9% due to higher commercial paper issuance for short-term liquidity management.
- Trading liabilities: Up 16% on higher short positions in debt instruments driven by Fixed Income Markets activity.
- Accounts payable and other liabilities: Up 19% due to higher client payables (including prime brokerage).
- Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs: Slightly down 1%.
- Long-term debt: Down 4% from fair value hedge accounting adjustments (higher rates) and lower fair value of structured notes in CIB, largely offset by net issuances in Treasury and CIO and CIB.
- Stockholders’ equity: Down 3% driven by net unrealized losses in AOCI from higher rates impacting the AFS portfolio and cash flow hedges.

Key themes and drivers
- Market volatility and client-driven market-making influenced trading assets/liabilities and securities financing.
- Rising interest rates impacted AFS valuations (AOCI), hedge accounting adjustments, MSR valuations, and funding mix.
- Strategic reclassification from AFS to HTM to manage OCI volatility.
- Loan growth across consumer and wholesale with corresponding increase in credit reserves amid a more adverse macro outlook and geopolitical risks.

title: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
heading: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
start_phrase:
The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in 
accordance with U.S. GAAP and this presentation is referred 
to as “reported” basis; these financial statements appear on 
page 88-92 .
summary:
- Purpose: Explains how the firm supplements U.S. GAAP (“reported”) results with non-GAAP (“managed”) measures and provides reconciliations between them.
- Key non-GAAP metrics used:
  - Firmwide managed-basis results (including FTE adjustments to make tax-advantaged income comparable to taxable, and the overhead ratio).
  - Pre-provision profit (total net revenue less total noninterest expense).
  - Net interest income (NII), net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets.
  - Tangible common equity (TCE), return on TCE (ROTCE), and tangible book value per share (TBVPS).
  - Adjusted expense (excluding Firmwide legal expense).
  - Allowance for loan losses to period-end loans retained (excluding trade finance and conduits).
- Reconciliation highlights (Q2 and first half 2022 vs 2021):
  - FTE adjustments increase total net revenue and pre-provision profit on a managed basis; overhead ratio improves on managed vs reported.
  - Provision for credit losses turned to a build in 2022 versus releases in 2021, reducing income before tax year-over-year.
  - Income tax expense is higher on a managed basis due to FTE; net income is unchanged by FTE adjustments.
- NII, yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets:
  - Managed NII rose year-over-year (Q2 up 19%; 1H up 13%), with higher net yields on average interest-earning assets.
  - Excluding Markets, NII grew faster (Q2 up 26%; 1H up 18%) and net yields were notably higher than total firm yields.
  - Noninterest revenue excluding Markets declined materially (Q2 down 26%; 1H down 21%), while total Markets net revenue increased (Q2 up 15%; 1H up 4%).
- TCE reconciliation:
  - TCE is derived by deducting goodwill and other intangibles and adding certain deferred tax liabilities to common stockholders’ equity.
  - Reported figures include period-end TCE around $204B at June 30, 2022; TBVPS of $69.53; ROTCE in 2022 below 2021 levels (e.g., Q2 2022 ~17% vs Q2 2021 ~23%).
- Footnotes/context:
  - FTE adjustments are recognized predominantly in CIB, CB, and Corporate; interest includes hedge effects.
  - References are provided to the firm’s 2021 Form 10-K for broader discussion and to another section for Markets details.

title: Description of business segment reporting methodology
heading: Description of business segment reporting methodology
start_phrase:
Results of the business segments are intended to present 
each segment as if it were a stand-alone business.
summary:
- The firm reports results by lines of business (LOB), with four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus a Corporate segment.
- Segments are defined by products/services and customer types and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance; results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis (see pages 18–19 for the definition and reconciliation).
- Segment reporting is designed to reflect each LOB as a stand-alone business, including allocations of certain income and expense items; assumptions, methodologies, and classifications are reviewed and refined periodically.
- Capital is assigned to each LOB as equity and reassessed at least annually; methodologies may change over time (see Line of business equity on page 47 and page 93 of the 2021 Form 10-K).
- Revenue sharing: when multiple segments collaborate on client transactions, revenue is recognized in the segment responsible for the product/service and allocated to participating segments per agreed sharing arrangements.
- Funds transfer pricing (FTP): allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and Other Corporate and transfers primary interest-rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO; FTP reflects risk characteristics of assets, liabilities, and off-balance sheet items and is updated periodically, which can change net interest income allocations.
- Foreign exchange risk: certain FX exposures from LOBs and Other Corporate are transferred to Treasury and CIO, which centrally manage and report FX impacts.
- Additional detail on business segment reporting methodology is provided in the 2021 Form 10-K (pages 61–62).
text:
Description of business segment reporting methodology
Results of the business segments are intended to present 
each segment as if it were a stand-alone business. The 
management reporting process that derives business 
segment results includes the allocation of certain income 
and expense items. The Firm periodically assesses the 
assumptions, methodologies and reporting classifications 
used for segment reporting, and further refinements may 
be implemented in future periods. The Firm also assesses 
the level of capital required for each LOB on at least an 
annual basis. The Firm’s LOBs also provide various business 
metrics which are utilized by the Firm and its investors and 
analysts in assessing performance. 
Revenue sharing 
When business segments join efforts to sell products and 
services to the Firm’s clients, the participating business 
segments may agree to share revenue from those 
transactions. Revenue is generally recognized in the 
segment responsible for the related product or service, with 
allocations to the other segment(s) involved in the 
transaction. The segment results reflect these revenue-
sharing agreements.Funds transfer pricing 
Funds transfer pricing (“FTP”) i s the process by which the 
Firm allocates interest income and expense to the LOBs and 
Other Corporate and transfers the primary interest rate risk 
and liquidity risk to Treasury and CIO. 
The funds transfer pricing process considers the interest 
rate risk and liquidity risk characteristics of assets and 
liabilities and off-balance sheet products. Periodically the 
methodology and assumptions utilized in the FTP process 
are adjusted to reflect economic conditions and other 
factors, which may impact the allocation of net interest 
income t o the segments.
Foreign exchange  risk
Foreign exchange risk is transferred  from the LOBs and 
Other Corporate to Treasury and CIO for certain revenues 
and expenses. Treasury and CIO manages these risks 
centrally and reports the impact of foreign exchange rate 
movements  related t o the transferred risk in its results .
Capital allocation
The amount of capital assigned to each business segment is 
referred to as equity. Periodically, the assumptions and 
methodologies used to allocate capital are reassessed and 
as a result, the capital allocated to the LOBs may change. 
Refer to Line of business equity on  page 47 , and  page 93 of 
JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for additional 
information on capital allocation.
Refer to Business Segment Results – Description of business 
segment reporting methodology on pages 61-62  of 
JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 10-K for a further discussion 
of those methodologies.

heading: 8.3.2 Quarterly results
start_phrase:
Net income was $3.1 billion , down 45% , reflecting an 
increase in the provision for credit losses compared with a 
net benefit in the prior year.
summary:
- Focus: Quarterly and year-to-date performance for a consumer banking segment, detailing income, revenue mix, expenses, and credit costs, with references to notes and risk management sections.

Quarterly results
- Net income: $3.1B, down 45%, primarily due to higher provision for credit losses versus a prior-year net benefit.
- Net revenue: $12.6B, down 1%.
- Net interest income (NII): $8.7B, up 8%.
  - Drivers: deposit growth in CBB and higher revolving Card loans.
  - Offsets: PPP loan forgiveness impact in CBB and lower Home Lending NII from tighter loan spreads.
- Noninterest revenue: $3.9B, down 17%.
  - Declines: lower Card income (higher amortization from new account origination costs and reduced interchange from a 4Q21 co-brand renegotiation), lower Home Lending production revenue (margins/volume), and lower Auto operating lease income (volume).
  - Offsets: higher net mortgage servicing revenue (MSR risk management gains from changed prepayment expectations and more third-party loans serviced) and higher deposit-related fees.
- Noninterest expense: $7.7B, up 9%.
  - Drivers: business investments and higher structural costs (compensation, technology, marketing).
  - Offset: lower volume/revenue-related expenses, mainly lower depreciation on reduced auto lease assets.
- Provision for credit losses: $761MM.
  - Net charge-offs: $611MM, down $121MM (strength in Card).
  - Allowance build: $150MM in Card due to loan growth.
  - Prior year included a $2.6B allowance reduction across CCB.
- References: Note 14 (MSR valuation/hedges; mortgage fees and related income) and Note 5 (card income); see Credit and Investment Risk Management (pp. 55–74) and Allowance for Credit Losses (pp. 71–73).

Year-to-date results
- Net income: $6.0B, down 52%, driven by higher provision vs. prior-year net benefit.
- Net revenue: $24.8B, down 2%.
- Net interest income: $17.0B, up 7%.
  - Drivers: deposit growth net of margin compression in CBB and higher revolving Card loans.
  - Offsets: PPP loan forgiveness impact in CBB and lower Home Lending NII from tighter spreads.
- Noninterest revenue: $7.8B, down 16%.
  - Declines: lower Home Lending production revenue (margins/volume), higher amortization for new Card account origination costs, and lower Auto operating lease income.
  - Offsets: higher net mortgage servicing revenue (MSR risk management gains and higher third-party servicing), higher travel-related commissions and asset management fees (net inflows), and higher deposit-related fees.
- Noninterest expense: $15.4B, up 8%.
  - Drivers: investments and higher structural costs (compensation, technology, marketing).
  - Offset: lower volume/revenue-related expenses, reflecting net decreases from lower auto lease depreciation and the impact of higher operating losses.
- Provision for credit losses: $1.4B.
  - Net charge-offs: $1.2B, down $591MM (strength in Card).
  - Allowance build: $275MM in Card and Home Lending.
  - Prior year included a $7.2B allowance reduction across CCB.

title: Quarterly results
heading: 8.4.2 Quarterly results
start_phrase: Net income was $3.7 billion , down 26% .
summary:
- Overview: The document presents quarterly and year-to-date financial results, highlighting performance across Banking, Markets & Securities Services, expenses, and credit provisions.

Quarterly highlights
- Net income $3.7B (down 26%); net revenue $11.9B (down 10%).
- Banking revenue $3.2B (down 37%).
  - Investment Banking $1.4B (down 61%) due to lower fees (down 54% across products) and $257M markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions.
    - Debt underwriting $741M (down 53%); Equity underwriting $245M (down 77%); Advisory $664M (down 28%).
  - Payments $1.5B (up 1%); excluding equity investment markdowns, $1.8B (up 25%) on stronger deposit margins and fees.
  - Lending $410M (up 79%) on fair value gains on loan hedge positions and higher net interest income.
- Markets & Securities Services revenue $8.7B (up 8%); Markets $7.8B (up 15%).
  - Fixed Income $4.7B (up 15%) with strength in macro (notably Currencies & Emerging Markets), partly offset by weaker Credit and Securitized Products.
  - Equity Markets $3.1B (up 15%) driven by derivatives.
  - Securities Services $1.2B (up 6%) on fee growth and better deposit margins, partly offset by lower market levels.
  - Credit Adjustments & Other: loss of $218M (vs. $233M gain prior year) mainly from funding spread widening.
- Noninterest expense $6.7B (up 3%) on higher structural costs and business investments, partly offset by lower revenue-related compensation.
- Provision for credit losses $59M, reflecting a modestly weaker macro outlook, partly offset by client-specific reserve reductions (vs. $79M net benefit prior year).
- References to detailed credit and ACL discussions on specified pages.

Year-to-date highlights
- Net income $8.1B (down 26%); net revenue $25.5B (down 8%).
- Banking revenue $7.5B (down 22%).
  - Investment Banking $3.4B (down 46%) on lower fees (down 44%) and $257M bridge financing markdowns in Q2; ranked #1 for Global IB fees (Dealogic).
    - Equity underwriting $494M (down 77%); Debt underwriting $1.7B (down 39%); Advisory $1.5B (down 8%).
  - Payments $3.3B (up 17%) on improved deposit margins, higher fees, and deposits.
  - Lending $731M (up 48%) on fair value gains on loan hedges and higher net interest income.
- Markets & Securities Services revenue $18.0B (down 1%); Markets $16.5B (up 4%).
  - Fixed Income $10.4B (up 6%) with macro strength offset by weaker Securitized Products and Credit.
  - Equity Markets $6.1B (up 3%) on derivatives and prime brokerage, partly offset by lower Cash Equities.
  - Securities Services $2.2B (up 4%) on fee growth and better deposit margins, offset by lower market levels.
  - Credit Adjustments & Other: loss of $742M, driven by funding spread widening and losses tied to commodities and Russia-related exposures (vs. $230M gain prior year).
- Noninterest expense $14.0B (up 3%) on higher structural costs, business investments, and legal expense, largely offset by lower volume- and revenue-related costs including compensation.
- Provision for credit losses $504M net addition, reflecting greater weighting of adverse scenarios, modest macro deterioration, and Russia-related downgrades in Q1 (vs. $410M net benefit prior year).

heading: 8.5.3 Quarterly results
start_phrase:
Net income was $994 million , down 30% , reflecting a net

summary:
- Quarterly results: Net income fell 30% to $994 million due to a shift from a prior-year net benefit to a net addition to the allowance for credit losses. Net revenue rose 8% to $2.7 billion. Net interest income increased 16% to $1.8 billion on higher deposit margins and loan growth, partly offset by higher funding costs. Noninterest revenue declined 5% to $904 million, driven by lower investment banking revenue and markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (primarily unfunded commitments), largely offset by a gain on an equity method investment received in partial satisfaction of a loan and higher payments revenue. Noninterest expense rose 18% to $1.2 billion on higher structural and volume-/revenue-related costs. Provision for credit losses was $209 million, a net addition driven largely by loan growth, versus a $377 million net benefit in the prior year.

- Year-to-date results: Net income decreased 29% to $1.8 billion, reflecting a higher provision for credit losses versus a prior-year net benefit. Net revenue increased 4% to $5.1 billion. Net interest income rose 10% to $3.3 billion on higher deposit margins and loan growth, partially offset by higher funding costs. Noninterest revenue fell 5% to $1.8 billion with the same drivers and offsets as the quarter. Noninterest expense increased 17% to $2.3 billion on higher structural and volume-/revenue-related costs. Provision for credit losses was $366 million, a net addition driven predominantly by loan growth, versus a $495 million net benefit in the prior year.

- The document cross-references Credit and Investment Risk Management (pages 55–74) and Allowance for Credit Losses (pages 71–73) for more detail.

title: Quarterly results
heading: 8.7.2 Quarterly results
start_phrase:
Net loss was $174 million , compared with a net loss of $1.3 
billion in the prior year.
summary:
- Focus: Corporate segment of JPMorgan Chase, including Treasury and CIO and Other Corporate, with selected income statement/balance sheet data for Q2 and first half of 2022 vs 2021, and commentary on results, drivers, taxes, FX, and international consumer growth initiatives.
- Results overview:
  - Net loss improved to $174 million in Q2 2022 from $1.3 billion in Q2 2021; year-to-date net loss improved to $1.0 billion from $2.1 billion.
  - Total net revenue was $80 million in Q2 2022 vs a loss of $1.2 billion; year-to-date net revenue was a loss of $801 million vs a loss of $1.6 billion.
  - Net interest income rose meaningfully, driven by higher rates and slower prepayments.
  - Provision for credit losses declined year-over-year for both the quarter and year-to-date.
- Noninterest revenue drivers:
  - Decreases due to U.S. dollar strengthening impacting FX-related revenues; higher net investment securities losses tied to portfolio repositioning (sales of U.S. Treasuries and U.S. GSE/government agency MBS); net losses including hedging costs on an equity method investment related to international consumer growth initiatives; and losses on certain legacy private equity investments year-to-date.
  - Offsets included net gains on certain legacy private equity investments in Q2 2022 vs prior-year losses; higher net gains on other Corporate investments; and an insurance settlement in Q1 2022.
- Expense trends:
  - Noninterest expense declined to $206 million in Q2 (down $309 million) and to $390 million year-to-date (down $1.0 billion), reflecting lower structural costs (including absence of prior-year contribution to the Firm’s Foundation), positive FX effects from a stronger U.S. dollar on certain expenses, lower technology and legal costs; partially offset by higher investment spending for international consumer growth initiatives.
- Taxes and methodology:
  - 2022 tax results driven by changes in the level/mix of taxable income/expenses and tax audit resolutions.
  - The Firm changed its internal income tax allocation methodology in Q1 2022 (no impact to Firmwide net income); prior periods revised for comparability.
  - Tax-equivalent adjustments included in total net revenue.
- Segment detail:
  - Treasury and CIO: Q2 2022 net revenue $82 million (vs -$1.1 billion) and net income $88 million (vs -$956 million); year-to-date net loss narrowed materially.
  - Other Corporate: Q2 2022 net revenue -$2 million (vs -$88 million) and net loss $262 million (vs $339 million); year-to-date net loss improved.
- Balance sheet and activity:
  - Total assets $1.46 trillion (+6% YoY); loans $2.2 billion (+43%); deposits $13.2 billion (predominantly tied to international consumer growth initiatives); headcount up 8% to 40,348.
- International consumer growth initiatives:
  - Includes Chase U.K. (digital retail bank), Nutmeg (U.K. digital wealth manager), and a 40% stake in Brazil’s C6 Bank (closed Q1 2022); associated revenues/expenses and hedging costs are highlighted as key drivers.
- Treasury and CIO investment securities portfolio:
  - Average portfolio size increased ~15% year-over-year; mix shifted from available-for-sale (AFS) to held-to-maturity (HTM) with significant transfers ($73.2 billion in Q2 2022; $104.5 billion in Q2 2021) for capital management.
  - Period-end portfolio net of allowance rose to $661.9 billion (+16% YoY); AFS down modestly; HTM up significantly.
  - Investment securities losses recognized in both periods (Q2 2022: -$153 million; year-to-date: -$547 million) tied to portfolio repositioning.
  - Average credit rating of the portfolio is AA+; small allowance for credit losses on securities.
- FX risk note: FX risk associated with certain revenues/expenses is transferred to Treasury and CIO; the net impact of FX movements was not material to net income.
- Cross-references: Points to other sections on Corporate overview, liquidity and funding risk, market risk (interest rate and FX), and investment securities disclosures.

title: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT - Introduction
heading: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT
start_phrase:
Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business 
activities.
summary: Introduction to JPMorgan Chase’s firmwide risk management, stating that risk is inherent in activities such as consumer/wholesale lending, investment advice, market-making, and other products/services. The objective is to manage businesses and associated risks to balance client, customer, and investor interests while protecting the Firm’s safety and soundness. Effective risk management requires individual responsibility for identifying and escalating risks, ownership of risk identification, assessment, data, and management within each line of business and Corporate, and firmwide risk governance structures. A disciplined, balanced compensation framework features strong internal governance and independent Board of Directors oversight, with risk and control issues factored into performance evaluations and incentive compensation.
text:
FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT 
Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business 
activities. When the Firm extends a consumer or wholesale 
loan, advises customers and clients on their investment 
decisions, makes markets in securities, or offers other                                                                                                                                                                                  
products or services, the Firm takes on some degree of risk. 
The Firm’s overall objective is to manage its businesses, and 
the associated risks, in a manner that balances serving the 
interests of its clients, customers and investors and protects 
the safety and soundness of the Firm. 
The Firm believes that effective risk management requires, 
among other things: 
•Acceptance of responsibility, including identification and 
escalation of risks by all individuals within the Firm; 
•Ownership of risk identification, assessment, data and 
management within each of the LOBs and Corporate; and 
•Firmwide structures for risk governance. 
The Firm follows a disciplined and balanced compensation 
framework with strong internal governance and 
independent oversight by the Board of Directors (the 
“Board”). The impact of risk and control issues is carefully 
considered in the Firm’s performance evaluation and 
incentive compensation processes.

title: Risk governance and oversight framework
heading: Risk governance and oversight framework
start_phrase:
The Firm’s risk management governance and oversight

heading: Basel III Overview
start_phrase:
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and 
internationally active U.S. Bank Holding Companies

summary:
- Defines capital risk as the sufficiency and composition of capital to support business activities in normal and stressed conditions, with references to the firm’s 10-K, 10-Q Note 21, and Pillar 3 disclosures for more detail.
- Basel III overview:
  - Capital adequacy based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) under two methods: Standardized and Advanced.
  - The firm’s Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding than its Advanced ratios.
  - Advanced Approaches firms must also meet the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR); the firm’s SLR is currently more binding than its Basel III Standardized risk-based ratios.
- Key regulatory developments:
  - CECL capital transition: Two-year delay expired 12/31/21; starting 1/1/22, the $2.9B CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years; $2.2B remained in CET1 as of 6/30/22. A 25% phase-out also applies to related Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure items.
  - Adoption of SA-CCR (effective 1/1/22) replacing the Current Exposure Method for derivatives exposure under both Standardized and Advanced RWAs (where models aren’t used) and for SLR. Impact: ~+$40B to Standardized RWA (as of 12/31/21 exposure), ~30 bps decrease in CET1 ratio, modest decrease in total leverage exposure; Advanced RWA also increased but less.

text:
Basel III Overview
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and 
internationally active U.S.  Bank Holding Companies  
(“BHCs ”) and banks, including the Firm and its insured 
depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries,  including 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. The minimum amount of 
regulatory capital that must be held by BHCs and banks is 
determined by calculating risk-weighted assets (“RWA”), 
which are on-balance sheet assets and off-balance sheet 
exposures, weighted according to risk. Two comprehensive 
approaches are prescribed for calculating RWA: a 
standardized approach (“Basel III Standardized”), and an 
advanced approach (“Basel III Advanced”). For each of the 
risk-based capital ratios, the capital adequacy of the Firm is 
evaluated against the lower of the Standardized or 
Advanced approac hes compared to their respective 
regulatory capital ratio requirements.  The Firm’s Basel III 
Standardized-risk-based ratios are currently more binding 
than the Basel III Advanced-risk-based ratios.  
Basel III also includes a requirement for Advanced 
Approaches banking organizations, including the Firm, to 
calculate the  SLR. The Firm’s SLR is currently more binding 
than the Basel III Standardized-risk-based ratios . Refer to 
SLR on page 47  for additional information.

text:
Key Regulatory Developments
CECL regulatory capital transition . On December 31, 2021, 
the CECL capital transition provisions ,	which delayed the 
effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, expired. 
Beginning January 1, 2022, the $ 2 . 9  b i l l i o n CECL capital 
benefit recognized as of December 31, 2021,  is being  
phased out at 25%  per year over a three-year period.  As of 
J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, CET1 capital reflected the remaining 
$ 2 . 2  b i l l i o n, benefit associated with the CECL capital 
transition provisions.
Additionally, effective January 1, 2022, the Firm phased 
out 25% of the other relevant CECL capital transition 
provisions recognized as of December 31, 2021, from Tier 
2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage 
exposure.  
Refer to Capital Risk Management on pages 86-96  and Note 
1 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for further 
information on CECL capital transition provisions and the 
CECL accounting guidance.Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk. On 
January 1, 2022, the Firm adopted “Standardized Approach 
for Counterpa r t y  C r e d i t  R i s k ”  ( “ S A - C C R ” ) ,  w h i c h  r e p l a c e d  
the Current Exposure Method used to measure derivatives 
counterparty exposure under the Standardized and 
Advanced approach RWA where internal models are not 
used, as well as leverage exposure used to calculate the SLR 
in the regulatory capital framework. The rule issued by the 
U.S. banking regulators in November 2019 applies to Basel 
III Advanced Approaches banking organizations, such as the 
Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
The adoption of SA-CCR on January 1, 2022 increased the 
Firm’s Standardized RWA by approximately $40 billion 
based on the Firm's derivatives exposure as of December 
31, 2021, which resulted in a decrease o f approximately 30 
bps to the Firm's C ET1 capital ratio and a modest decrease 
in its total leverage exp osure. In addition, the adoption of 
SA-CCR increased the Firm's Advanced RWA, but to a lesser 
extent than Standardized .

- Focus: Regulatory capital under Basel III. Reconciliations from GAAP stockholders’ equity to CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital, Tier 2 capital, and Total capital under both Standardized and Advanced approaches as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, plus a six‑month capital rollforward.

- CET1 reconciliation:
  - Start with total stockholders’ equity; subtract preferred stock to get common equity.
  - Add certain deferred tax liabilities related to tax‑deductible goodwill/intangibles and other CET1 adjustments (including the CECL transition benefit).
  - Deduct goodwill and other intangible assets.
  - Resulting CET1: $207.4B at 6/30/22 vs. $213.9B at 12/31/21.

- Tier 1 capital:
  - Add preferred stock to CET1 and subtract other Tier 1 adjustments.
  - Notes include a $2.0B Series Z preferred stock called at 12/31/21 and redeemed 2/1/22.
  - Resulting Tier 1: $239.7B at 6/30/22 vs. $246.2B at 12/31/21.

- Tier 2 capital:
  - Components include qualifying long‑term debt and instruments, qualifying allowance for credit losses (ACL) subject to RWA caps and CECL transition effects, and other adjustments.
  - Standardized Tier 2: $28.6B at 6/30/22 vs. $28.7B at 12/31/21.
  - Advanced Tier 2 reflects an adjustment for the excess of eligible credit reserves over expected losses (capped at 0.6% of credit risk RWA): $17.6B at 6/30/22 vs. $19.6B at 12/31/21.

- Total capital:
  - Standardized Total capital: $268.3B at 6/30/22 vs. $274.9B at 12/31/21.
  - Advanced Total capital: $257.3B at 6/30/22 vs. $265.8B at 12/31/21.

- Key footnotes and clarifications:
  - Deferred tax liabilities tied to tax‑deductible goodwill/intangibles are netted in CET1.
  - CECL capital transition provided a CET1 benefit of $2.2B at 6/30/22 and $2.9B at 12/31/21; it also affects ACL eligibility in Tier 2.
  - ACL eligible for inclusion up to 1.25% of credit risk RWA (Standardized) and excess reserves up to 0.6% of RWA (Advanced).
  - Goodwill includes equity method goodwill from the C6 Bank investment.
  - AOCI components referenced include cash flow hedges and DVA on structured notes.

- Capital rollforward (six months ended 6/30/22):
  - CET1 decreased by $6.5B (to $207.4B), driven primarily by a $14.3B decline in AOCI and other CET1 adjustments (−$2.8B), partially offset by net income of $16.1B; dividends (−$5.9B), treasury stock repurchases (−$2.1B), APIC (+$0.2B), and an AOCI adjustment (+$2.3B).
  - Tier 1 decreased by $6.5B to $239.7B; no net issuance of preferred stock; minor other changes.
  - Standardized Tier 2 was roughly flat (−$0.1B) with lower qualifying debt (−$1.9B) offset by higher ACL (+$2.1B) and other (−$0.3B).
  - Advanced Tier 2 declined by $2.0B to $17.6B.
  - Ending totals: Standardized Total capital $268.3B; Advanced Total capital $257.3B.

summary:
- RWA rollforward: For the six months ended June 30, 2022, the firm presents Basel III Standardized and Advanced RWA movements, showing:
  - Standardized total RWA increased to $1,704.9B from $1,638.9B (+$66.0B), driven by portfolio level movements (+$76.5B) partially offset by model & data changes (–$10.5B). Credit risk RWA rose to $1,596.8B; Market risk RWA rose to $108.1B.
  - Advanced total RWA increased to $1,613.2B from $1,547.9B (+$65.3B), with portfolio level movements (+$67.3B) offset by model & data changes (–$2.0B). Credit risk RWA rose to $1,079.8B; Market risk RWA rose to $108.3B; Operational risk RWA rose to $425.1B.
  - Drivers and definitions: Model & data changes reflect methodology/treatment updates per regulatory guidance (excluding rule changes). Portfolio movements (inclusive of rule changes) include SA-CCR adoption (effective Jan 1, 2022), changes in book size and composition/credit quality, market movements, position rolloffs (e.g., Home Lending), and for Operational risk RWA, updates to cumulative losses and macro inputs.
  - Off-balance sheet RWA within Credit risk: Standardized $212.4B at 6/30/22 vs $218.5B at 12/31/21; Advanced $181.6B vs $188.5B.
  - References to Pillar 3 Regulatory Capital Disclosures for further detail on Credit, Market, and Operational risk RWA.

- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR): Components and results as of 6/30/22 vs 12/31/21:
  - Tier 1 capital $239.7B vs $246.2B.
  - Total average assets $3.912T vs $3.832T; after regulatory capital adjustments, adjusted average assets $3.862T vs $3.782T.
  - Off-balance sheet exposures $701.1B vs $789.8B (includes SA-CCR impact effective Jan 1, 2022).
  - Total leverage exposure $4.563T vs $4.572T.

  - Notes: Regulatory capital adjustments include deductions for items like goodwill and CECL transition; off-balance sheet exposures are based on average of month-end balances. Additional SLR background referenced to the 2021 Form 10-K.

- Line of business equity (allocated capital): Capital allocated by segment reflects peer capital levels and regulatory requirements.

  - Corporate & Investment Bank: $103.0B (up from $83.0B).
  - Commercial Banking: $25.0B (up from $24.0B).
  - Asset & Wealth Management: $17.0B (up from $14.0B).
  - Corporate: $58.3B (down from $88.3B).
  - Total common stockholders’ equity: $253.3B (down from $259.3B).
  - Further details referenced to the 2021 Form 10-K.

summary:
- Capital actions overview, including common and preferred equity activity, regulatory capital planning, and compliance with loss-absorbing capacity rules.
- Common stock dividends: Quarterly dividend of $1.00 per share, subject to Board approval.
- Common stock repurchases: Prior $30B authorization through April 30, 2022; new $30B authorization effective May 1, 2022. Share repurchases temporarily suspended due to the expected increase in the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) in Q4 2022 and GSIB surcharge in Q1 2023. Reported buybacks: Q2 2022 vs. Q2 2021 (5.0M shares/$622M vs. 39.5M/$6.2B) and 1H 2022 vs. 1H 2021 (23.1M/$3.1B vs. 74.2M/$11.2B). Note on 2021 Fed restrictions limiting combined dividends and repurchases in H1 2021.

text:
Capital planning and stress testing
Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review
On April 5, 2022, the Firm submitted its 2022 Capital Plan 
to the Federal Reserve. On June 27, 2022, the Firm 
announced that it had completed the Federal Reserve's 
2022 Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (“CCAR”) 
stress test process. The Firm's indicative SCB requirement  is 
4.0% (up from the current 3.2%), which will result in a  
Standardized CET1 capital ratio requirement, including 
regulatory buffers, of 12.0% (up from the current 11.2%). 
The Federal Reserve will provide the Firm with its final SCB 
requirement by August 31, 2022, and that requirement will 
become effective on October 1, 2022, and will remain in 
effect until September 30, 2023 .
Refer to Capital planning and stress testing on pages 86-87  
of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 10-K for additional 
information on CCAR.

summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase’s liquidity risk management framework, definitions, regulatory metrics, and available liquidity sources.
- Liquidity risk defined as the risk of not meeting obligations or lacking appropriate funding mix and tenor; references to 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports.
- LCR and HQLA:
  - Minimum LCR requirement of 100% for both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - Excess HQLA held at the Bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from Firm-level eligible HQLA.
  - Average LCR metrics (three months ended):
    - JPMorgan Chase & Co.:
      - LCR: 110% (Jun 30, 2022), 110% (Mar 31, 2022), 111% (Jun 30, 2021)
      - Total HQLA: $741,953m; $722,515m; $716,556m
      - Eligible cash: $634,480m; $680,003m; $673,724m
      - Eligible securities: $107,473m; $42,512m; $42,832m
      - Net cash outflows: $676,234m; $658,998m; $647,757m
      - Net excess eligible HQLA: $65,719m; $63,517m; $68,799m
    - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.:
      - LCR: 169%; 181%; 171%
      - Net excess eligible HQLA: $487,867m; $560,987m; $489,311m
  - Notes: Eligible cash primarily central bank deposits; eligible securities include U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds (net of LCR haircuts); eligible HQLA may be recorded across several balance sheet lines.
  - Bank’s average LCR fell in Q2 2022 vs. Q1 2022 due to lower HQLA from loan-driven cash reductions and declines in market values of HQLA-eligible securities in Treasury and CIO; references Note 9 for unrealized gains/losses. LCR fluctuates with changes in HQLA and net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.
- Other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities (including excess eligible HQLA at the Bank not transferable to non-bank affiliates): fair value ~$826B (Jun 30, 2022) vs. ~$914B (Dec 31, 2021), primarily lower due to reduced excess eligible HQLA at the Bank; realizable liquidity depends on market conditions.

  - Requirement to maintain available stable funding ≥ required stable funding over a one-year horizon; 100% minimum.

LCR and HQLA
The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible  HQLA that is 
sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash 
outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of 
significant stress.  Under the LCR rule, the amount of eligible 
HQLA held by JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that is in excess of 
its stand-alone 100% minimum LCR requirement, and that 
is not transferable to non-bank affiliates, must be excluded 
from the Firm’s reported eligible HQLA.  The LCR for both 
the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is required to be a 
minimum of 100%.  Refer to page 98  of JPMorgan Chase’s

title: Other liquidity sources
heading: Other liquidity sources
start_phrase:
In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible 
HQLA discussed above, the Firm had unencumbered 
marketable securities, such as equity and debt securities, 
that the Firm believes would be available to raise liquidity.
summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for further detail.
- Explains LCR and HQLA framework:
  - Both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain a minimum 100% LCR, holding eligible HQLA sufficient to cover 30 days of stressed net cash outflows.
  - Excess eligible HQLA at the Bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported eligible HQLA.
  - References additional detail on HQLA and net cash outflows on page 98 of the 2021 Form 10-K.
- Reports average LCR metrics for the three months ended June 30, 2022, March 31, 2022, and June 30, 2021:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR ~110% across periods; Q2 2022 HQLA $742B (eligible cash $634B; eligible securities $107B), net cash outflows $676B, net excess eligible HQLA $66B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 169% in Q2 2022 (down from 181% in Q1 2022; 171% in Q2 2021); net excess eligible HQLA $488B in Q2 2022.
  - Notes on composition: eligible cash is primarily central bank deposits; eligible securities mainly U.S. Treasuries, GSE/agency MBS, and sovereigns; HQLA securities may appear across multiple balance sheet line items.
- Highlights drivers and variability:
  - The Bank’s average LCR decreased in Q2 2022 versus Q1 2022 due to reduced cash from loan growth and declines in market values of HQLA-eligible investment securities in Treasury and CIO.
  - LCRs fluctuate with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.
- Other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities that could be used to raise liquidity totaled about $826B at June 30, 2022 (down from $914B at December 31, 2021), largely due to lower excess eligible HQLA at the Bank.
  - Additional borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window was approximately $308B at both June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, based on pledged collateral; the discount window is not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- NSFR:
  - Describes requirement to maintain sufficient “available” stable funding relative to “required” stable funding over a one-year horizon.
  - Confirms the Firm and the Bank met the 100% minimum NSFR as of June 30, 2022.
  - Notes semiannual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will begin in 2023.
text:
Other liquidity sources
In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible 
HQLA discussed above, the Firm had unencumbered 
marketable securities, such as equity and debt securities, 
that the Firm believes would be available to raise liquidity. 
This includes excess eligible HQLA securities at JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A. that are not transferable to non-bank 
affiliates. The fair value of these securities was 
approximately $826 billion  and $914 billion  as of J u n e  3 0 ,  
2022  and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, respectively , although the 
amount of liquidity that could be raised at any particular 
time would be dependent on prevailing market conditions.  
The fair value decreased compared to December 31, 2021, 
primarily due to a de crease  in excess eligible HQLA at 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., as noted above.
The Firm also had available borrowing capacity at the  
Federal Home Loan Banks (“FHLBs”) and the discount 
window at the Federal Reserve Bank as a result of collateral 
pledged by the Firm to such banks of approximately $308 
billion  as of  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2 and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1. This 
borrowing capacity excludes the benefit of cash and 
securities reported in the Firm’s eligible HQLA or other 
unencumbered securities that are currently pledged at the 
Federal Reserve Bank discount window and other central 
banks.  Although available,  the Firm does not view this 
borrowing capacity at the Federal Reserve Bank discount 
window and the other central banks as a primary source of 
liquidity.

title: NSFR
heading: NSFR
start_phrase:

summary:

NSFR
The net stable funding ratio (“NSFR”) rule requires that the 
Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of 
“available” stable funding that is sufficient to meet their

title: Funding
heading: Funding
start_phrase:
Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and 
secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and 
off-balance sheet obligations, which includes both short- 
and long-term cash requirements.
summary:
- Topic: Firm’s funding sources and deposit trends.
- Funding strategy: Management asserts sufficient unsecured and secured funding capacity to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations. The Firm uses diversified funding: stable deposits, secured and unsecured capital markets funding, and stockholders’ equity.
- Entity-specific funding:
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: Primarily funded by deposits; can access short- and long-term secured borrowings, issue unsecured long-term debt, or borrow from the Intermediate Holding Company (IHC).
  - Non-bank subsidiaries: Funded mainly via long-term unsecured borrowings and short-term secured borrowings (including securities lending and repurchase agreements).
- Liquidity deployment: Excess funding is invested by Treasury and CIO in investment securities or placed in cash/short-term liquid assets based on interest rate and liquidity risk.
- Deposits as stable funding: Consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits are highlighted as stable due to operating relationships.
- Deposit levels (by LOB and total):
  - Total Firm deposits at period-end: $2,471.5B (Jun 30, 2022) vs $2,462.3B (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Average deposits:
    - Three months ended Jun 30: $2,532.3B (2022) vs $2,323.8B (2021).
    - Six months ended Jun 30: $2,524.0B (2022) vs $2,274.5B (2021).
  - LOB period-end (Jun 30, 2022 vs Dec 31, 2021): CCB $1,178.8B vs $1,148.1B; CIB $738.8B vs $707.8B; CB $283.3B vs $324.0B; AWM $257.4B vs $282.1B; Corporate $13.2B vs $0.4B.
- Balance sheet ratios:
  - Deposits as % of total liabilities: 70% (Jun 30, 2022) vs 71% (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Loans: $1,104.2B (Jun 30, 2022) vs $1,077.7B (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Loans-to-deposits ratio: 45% (Jun 30, 2022) vs 44% (Dec 31, 2021).
- Trends and drivers:
  - Average deposits increased year-over-year for both the three- and six-month periods ended Jun 30, 2022, largely reflecting residual effects of prior-year government actions.
  - CCB growth supported by new and existing consumer and small business accounts.
  - In 2Q22, deposits declined in certain areas: CB due to migration of non-operating deposits into higher-yielding alternatives; CCB due to increased consumer spending.
  - Corporate deposit increases tied to international consumer growth initiatives.
- References: Note 22 for off-balance sheet obligations; further deposit/liability trends in Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis and Business Segment Results sections.
text:
Funding 
Sources of funds
Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and 
secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and 
off-balance sheet obligations, which includes both short- 
and long-term cash requirements.
The Firm funds its global balance sheet through diverse 
sources of funding including stable deposits, secured and 
unsecured funding in the capital markets and stockholders’ 
equity. Deposits are the primary funding source for 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. Additionally, JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. may access funding through short- or long-term 
secured borrowings, through the issuance of unsecured long-term debt, or from borrowings from  the Intermediate 
Holding Company (“IHC”). The Firm’s non-bank subsidiaries 
are primarily funded from long-term unsecured borrowings 
and short-term secured borrowings, primarily securities 
loaned or sold under repurchase agreements. Excess 
funding is invested by  Treasury and CIO  in the Firm’s 
investment securities portfolio or deployed in cash or other 
short-term liquid investments based on their interest rate 
and liquidity risk characteristics.  
Refer to Note 22 for additional information on off-balance 
sheet obligations.

title: Short-term funding
heading: Short-term funding
start_phrase:
The Firm’s sources of short-term secured funding primarily 
consist of securities loaned or sold under agreements to 
repurchase.
summary:
- Scope: Summarizes the firm’s non-deposit funding mix as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, plus average balances for the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, with cross-references to other 10-Q and 10-K sections.
- Short-term unsecured funding: Comprised mainly of commercial paper, other borrowed funds, and federal funds purchased. Commercial paper outstanding and average balances increased versus year-end 2021 and prior-year periods, driven by higher net issuance for short-term liquidity management.
- Short-term secured funding: Dominated by securities sold under agreements to repurchase and securities loaned, plus other borrowed funds and obligations of firm-administered multi-seller conduits. Repos rose at June 30, 2022 versus December 31, 2021 due to higher secured financing of trading assets and netting effects from client-driven market-making, partially offset by lower secured financing of AFS investment securities in Treasury and CIO.
- Collateral quality: Short-term secured funding is backed predominantly by high-quality collateral, including government-issued debt and U.S. GSE and agency MBS.
- Balance dynamics: Secured funding balances fluctuate with client investment/financing activity, the firm’s financing demand, liability-mix management between secured and unsecured funding, and market/portfolio factors.
- Long-term unsecured funding: Includes senior notes, subordinated debt, and structured notes (some TLAC-eligible). Totals modestly declined from year-end 2021 to June 30, 2022.
- Long-term secured funding: Includes credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and other long-term secured funding (including secured long-term structured notes).
- Equity: Presents preferred stock and common stockholders’ equity balances, with references to detailed capital risk management and stockholders’ equity disclosures.
- Consolidation/VIE notes: Obligations of multi-seller conduits and credit card securitizations are included in beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs. Structured notes include certain TLAC-eligible parent company long-term debt.
- Key quantitative highlights at June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021:
  - Total short-term unsecured funding: $33.7B vs. $26.9B (increase, led by commercial paper: $21.7B vs. $15.1B).
  - Total short-term secured funding: $254.4B vs. $227.3B (increase, mainly repos).
  - Total long-term unsecured funding: $273.4B vs. $286.0B (slight decrease).
  - Total long-term secured funding: $16.6B vs. $17.4B (slight decrease).
  - Preferred stock: $32.8B; Common stockholders’ equity: $253.3B (point-in-time figures shown alongside averages).

title: Long-term funding and issuance
heading: Long-term funding and issuance

summary:
- Focus: The section explains the Firm’s long-term funding strategy, sources, issuance activity, and maturities/redemptions for both unsecured and secured funding, with comparisons for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.

- Strategy and objectives:
  - Long-term funding is used to provide stable funding and liquidity.
  - The plan is driven by expected client activity, liquidity needs, and regulatory requirements, including TLAC.
  - Objectives include diversification, maximizing market access, and optimizing funding costs, with evaluation across markets, tenors, and currencies.

- Funding structure:
  - The significant majority of long-term unsecured funding is issued by the Parent Company, which advances substantially all net proceeds to the IHC; the IHC does not issue external debt.
  - Some structured notes issued by the Parent Company are TLAC-eligible.

- Long-term unsecured funding activity (Q2 and H1 2022 vs. 2021):
  - Parent Company:
    - Issuance: $13.9bn in Q2 2022 ($24.2bn in Q2 2021); $25.9bn in H1 2022 ($37.8bn in H1 2021).
    - Maturities/redemptions: $5.4bn in Q2 2022 ($5.8bn in Q2 2021); $10.1bn in H1 2022 ($10.5bn in H1 2021).
    - Mix includes senior notes (U.S. and non-U.S.) and structured notes.
  - Subsidiaries:
    - Issuance is entirely structured notes: $11.2bn in Q2 2022 ($7.3bn in Q2 2021); $19.7bn in H1 2022 ($17.8bn in H1 2021).
    - Maturities/redemptions: $7.4bn in Q2 2022 ($9.7bn in Q2 2021); $15.1bn in H1 2022 ($18.2bn in H1 2021).

- Long-term secured funding:
  - Sources include securitization of consumer credit card loans, FHLB advances, and other secured long-term structured notes.
  - 2022 activity was modest:
    - Q2 2022: $82m issuance; $35m maturities/redemptions.
    - H1 2022: $284m issuance; $748m maturities/redemptions (including $650m of credit card securitization maturities).
  - Client-driven securitizations by wholesale businesses are excluded as they are not a source of Firm funding.

- Cross-references: Points to Liquidity Risk Management and 2021 Form 10-K notes for more detail on the IHC, long-term debt, and client-driven securitizations.

Long-term funding and issuance
Long-term funding provides an additional source of stable funding and liquidity for the Firm. The Firm’s long-term funding plan

evaluates various funding markets, tenors and currencies in creating its optimal long-term funding plan.  
The significant majority of the Firm’s long-term unsecured funding is issued by the Parent Company to provide flexibility in 
support of both bank and non-bank subsidiary funding needs.  The Parent Company advances substantially all net funding 
proceeds to its subsidiary, the IHC. The IHC does not issue debt to external counterparties.  The following table summarizes

heading: Credit ratings
start_phrase:

- Explains that credit ratings materially affect the Firm’s cost and availability of funding; downgrades could limit access to liquidity, increase funding costs, trigger additional collateral or funding requirements, and reduce the pool of willing investors and counterparties.
- Notes that the impact of downgrades varies by contractual and behavioral factors and is incorporated into the Firm’s liquidity risk management and stress testing; the Firm believes it holds sufficient liquidity to withstand reduced funding capacity from potential downgrades.
- Indicates that downgrades may also adversely affect funding needs for VIEs and other third‑party commitments; directs readers to Note 4 for details on liquidity risk and credit‑related contingent features tied to VIEs, derivatives, and collateral agreements.
- Provides the long‑ and short‑term issuer ratings and outlooks as of June 30, 2022 from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch for the Parent and principal bank and non‑bank subsidiaries (including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; J.P. Morgan Securities plc; and J.P. Morgan SE). Highlights include:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: Moody’s A2/P‑1 (positive long‑term, stable short‑term outlooks), S&P A‑/A‑2 (Positive), Fitch AA‑/F1+ (Stable).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: Moody’s Aa2/P‑1 (Stable), S&P A+/A‑1 (Positive), Fitch AA/F1+ (Stable).
  - J.P. Morgan Securities LLC: Moody’s Aa3/P‑1 (Stable), S&P A+/A‑1 (Positive), Fitch AA/F1+ (Stable).

text:
Credit ratings
The cost and availability of financing are influenced by 
credit ratings. Reductions in these ratings could have an 
adverse effect on the Firm’s access to liquidity sources, 
increase the cost of funds, trigger additional collateral or 
funding requirements and decrease the number of investors 
and counterparties willing to lend to the Firm. The nature 
and magnitude of the impact of ratings downgrades 
depends on numerous contractual and behavioral factors, 
which the Firm believes are incorporated in its liquidity risk 
and stress testing metrics. The Firm believes that it 
maintains sufficient liquidity to withstand a potential 
decrease in funding capacity due to ratings downgrades.Additionally, the Firm’s funding requirements for VIEs and 
other third-party commitments may be adversely affected 
by a decline in credit ratings. Refer to liquidity risk and 
credit-related contingent features in Note 4 for additional 
information on the impact of a credit ratings downgrade on 
the funding requirements for VIEs, and on derivatives and 
collateral agreements.

summary:
- Scope: Consumer lending portfolio excluding credit cards, with emphasis on residential real estate.
- Overall trend: Total loans declined since Dec 31, 2021, driven by decreases in residential real estate loans measured at fair value and in auto/other loans, partly offset by higher retained residential mortgage balances.
- Residential real estate composition: Predominantly prime first-lien mortgages and home equity lines of credit (HELOCs).
- Retained mortgages: Balances increased net of paydowns; nonaccrual retained loans fell due to improved credit performance. Net recoveries were lower in Q2 2022 versus prior year on reduced prepayments from higher rates; first-half net recoveries were roughly flat year over year.
- Loans at fair value: Decreased as Home Lending warehouse loan sales outpaced originations amid higher rates and lower loan purchase activity in CIB; nonaccrual fair value loans also declined, driven by CIB.
- HELOCs: $16.9B outstanding at June 30, 2022, including $5.5B recast/modified and $5.5B interest-only balloon HELOCs maturing mostly after 2030; risk managed by closing/reducing undrawn lines when borrower credit deteriorates.
- Interest-only mortgages: $34.4B at June 30, 2022 (up from $30.0B), typically higher-balance AWM borrowers; Q2 2022 showed net charge-offs due to a loan sale; 1H 2022 showed net recoveries; credit performance comparable to the broader prime portfolio.
- Government-insured/guaranteed mortgages: $1.158B at June 30, 2022 (down from $1.447B), with current $584M, 30–89 days past due $121M, and 90+ days past due $453M; allowance incorporates exposure to potential unrecoverable claim payments.
- Modified residential mortgages: Retained modified loans to borrowers in financial difficulty (including TDRs and certain modified PCD loans) totaled $12.185B (down from $13.251B); nonaccrual retained modified loans were $3.543B (down from $3.938B). Includes $2.8B (vs. $2.7B) of nonaccrual TDRs less than 90 days past due.
- Additional references: Note 11 for geographic and LTV details; prior Form 10-K for TDR nonaccrual treatment.

text:
WHOLESALE CREDIT PORTFOLIO
In its wholesale businesses, the Firm is exposed to credit 
risk primarily through its underwriting, lending, market-
making, and hedging activities with and for clients and 
counterparties, as well as through various operating 
services (such as cash management and clearing activities), 
securities financing activities and cash placed with banks. A 
portion of the loans originated or acquired by the Firm’s 
wholesale businesses is generally retained on the balance 
sheet. The Firm distributes a significant percentage of the 
loans that it originates into the market as part of its 
syndicated loan business and to manage portfolio 
concentrations and credit risk. The wholesale portfolio is 
actively managed, in part by conducting ongoing, in-depth 
reviews of client credit quality and transaction structure 
inclusive of collateral where applicable, and of industry, 
product and client concentrations. Refer to the industry 
discussion on pages 64-67  for further information.
The Firm’s wholesale credit portfolio includes exposure held 
in CIB, CB, AWM and Corporate, as well as risk-rated 
exposures held in CCB, including business banking and auto 
dealer exposure for which the wholesale methodology is 
applied when determining the allowance for credit losses.
In the six months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, credit continued to 
perform well with charge-offs at historically low level s. As 
of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, the decrease in n onperforming exposure 
was driven by a decline in lending related commitments as 
a result of net portfolio activity, predominantly in CIB, 
partially offset by an increase in nonperforming derivatives. 
Nonperforming loans were relatively flat and included 
paydowns on exposures to certain Russia an d Russia-
associated clients that were downgraded in the first quarter 
of 2022 . Refer to Business Developments on page 9 and 
Country Risk on pages 80-81  for additional information.

heading: 9.5.3.1 Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
start_phrase:

summary:
- Focus: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale credit exposure by maturity and internal risk ratings as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Investment-grade definition: Internal ratings qualitatively equivalent to BBB-/Baa3 or higher; collateral and structural support are considered in assigning internal ratings. Cross-reference to 2021 Form 10-K Note 12.
- Components covered:
  - Loans retained (by maturity buckets: ≤1 year, 1–5 years, >5 years; and by ratings: investment-grade vs non-investment-grade).
  - Derivative receivables net of liquid securities and cash collateral (by maturity and ratings).
  - Lending-related commitments (by maturity and ratings).
  - Subtotal of the above, plus loans held-for-sale/at fair value and receivables from customers, to arrive at total exposure net of derivative collateral.
  - Credit derivatives and credit-related notes used in credit portfolio management (not qualifying for hedge accounting), shown by maturity and ratings of the reference entities; notional amounts presented on a net basis.
- Key figures and trends:
  - Total wholesale credit exposure (net of derivative collateral) increased to $1.23 trillion at 6/30/22 from $1.19 trillion at 12/31/21.
  - Loans retained rose to $584.3 billion (72% investment-grade) from $560.4 billion (73% IG).
  - Derivative receivables net of collateral increased to $61.5 billion (72% IG) from $47.0 billion (68% IG).
  - Lending-related commitments were broadly flat at ~$487.5 billion (68% IG both periods).
  - Subtotal of primary exposures increased to $1.133 trillion, with the investment-grade share modestly lower (70% vs 71% prior).
  - Loans held-for-sale/at fair value declined to $37.2 billion (from $39.8 billion); receivables from customers edged down to $58.3 billion (from $59.6 billion).
- Maturity profile: Exposure is concentrated in the 1–5 year bucket, with meaningful amounts also due within 1 year; smaller portion extends beyond 5 years in both periods.
- Credit portfolio management:
  - Net purchased credit protection via credit derivatives and credit-related notes decreased to $15.4 billion notional (from $18.7 billion).
  - Majority of reference entities are investment-grade (83% at 6/30/22 vs 80% at 12/31/21); counterparties for purchased protection are predominantly investment-grade.
- Methodology/footnotes:
  - Maturities are based on remaining contractual maturity; derivative receivables can become payable before stated maturity due to cash flows/market changes.
  - Loans held-for-sale primarily include syndicated loans and transfers from the retained portfolio.
  - Prior-period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.

The Firm focuses on the management and diversification of its industry exposures, and pays particular attention to industries
