heading: Consolidated statements of cash flows (unaudited) for the six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021
start_phrase: The Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (unaudited) are an integral part of these statements.
summary:
- Document scope: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s unaudited Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows for the six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, plus Note 1 (Basis of Presentation) from the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, with cross-references to the 2021 Form 10-K and a glossary.

- Cash flows (six months ended June 30):
  - Operating activities: Net cash provided of $24.1B in 2022 vs net cash used of $(30.3)B in 2021. Key drivers include net income ($16.9B vs $26.2B), a swing in provision for credit losses (expense of $2.6B vs benefit of $(6.4)B), significant loan held-for-sale activity (originations/purchases vs sales/securitizations), and large movements in trading assets/liabilities, receivables, and payables.
  - Investing activities: Net cash used of $(125.8)B in 2022 vs net cash provided of $33.1B in 2021, reflecting substantial activity in HTM/AFS securities (purchases, paydowns, sales), changes in federal funds sold and reverse repos, loan sales/securitizations, and other loan changes.
  - Financing activities: Net cash provided of $49.0B in 2022 vs $181.0B in 2021, driven by changes in deposits, repos, short- and long-term borrowings, capital actions (preferred stock issuance/redemption, treasury stock repurchases), and dividends.
  - FX effect on cash: $(18.8)B in 2022 vs $(5.9)B in 2021.
  - Net change in cash: Decrease of $(71.6)B in 2022 vs increase of $177.8B in 2021; ending cash and due from banks/deposits with banks of $669.3B (2022) vs $705.4B (2021).
  - Cash interest paid: $4.5B (2022) vs $2.5B (2021). Cash income taxes paid, net: $3.1B (2022) vs $13.7B (2021).

- Note 1 – Basis of presentation:
  - Firm overview: JPMorgan Chase is a U.S.-based financial holding company with global operations across investment banking, consumer/small business banking, commercial banking, transaction processing, and asset management; see Note 25 for segment details.
  - Reporting framework: Statements prepared under U.S. GAAP and applicable regulatory guidelines; interim unaudited financials include normal recurring adjustments; use of estimates; actual results may differ; should be read with the 2021 Form 10-K. Certain prior-period amounts reclassified for consistency.
  - Consolidation principles: Includes entities where the Firm has a controlling financial interest, assessed via voting interest entity vs variable interest entity (VIE) models; elimination of all material intercompany balances/transactions; client assets held in agency/fiduciary capacity are off-balance sheet. Further detail in 2021 Form 10-K Notes 1 and 14.
  - Offsetting policy: Derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral, and certain securities financing activities, presented on a net basis when legally enforceable master netting agreements exist; the Firm has elected to net where conditions are met; see 2021 Form 10-K for details.

Basis of presentation
JPMorgan Chase  & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”), a 
financial holding company incorporated under Delaware law 
in 1968, is a leading financial services firm based in the 
U.S., with operations worldwide. The Firm is a leader in 
investment banking, financial services for consumers and 
small businesses, commercial banking, financial transaction 
processing and asset management. Refer to Note 25 for a 
further discussion of the Firm’s business segments.
The accounting and financial reporting policies of  JPMorgan 
Chase  and its subsidiaries conform to  U.S. GAAP. 
Additionally, where applicable, the policies conform to the 
accounting and reporting guidelines prescribed by 
regulatory authorities.  
The unaudited Consolidated Financial Statements prepared 
in conformity with U.S. GAAP require management to make 
estimates and assumptions that affect the reported 
amounts of assets, liabilities, revenue and expense, and the 
disclosures of contingent assets and liabilities. Actual 
results could be different from these estimates. In the 
opinion of management, all normal, recurring adjustments 
have been included such that this interim financial 
information is fairly stated.
These unaudited Consolidated Financial Statements should 
be read in conjunction with the audited Consolidated 
Financial Statements, and related notes thereto, included in  
JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021  Form 10-K.
Certain amounts reported in prior periods have been 
reclassified to conform with the current presentation.

Consolidation 
The Consolidated Financial Statements include the accounts 
of JPMorgan Chase and other entities in which  the Firm has 
a controlling financial interest. All material intercompany 
balances and transactions  have been eliminated.
Assets held for clients in an agency or fiduciary capacity by  
the Firm are not assets of  JPMorgan Chase and are not 
included on the Consolidated balance sheets.
The Firm determines whether it has a controlling financial 
interest in an entity by first evaluating whether the entity is 
a voting interest entity or a variable interest entity.  
Refer to Notes  1 and 14 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 
10-K for a further description of  JPMorgan Chase’s 
accounting policies regarding consolidation.

Offsetting assets and liabilities
U.S. GAAP permits entities to present derivative receivables 
and derivative payables with the same counterparty and the 
related cash collateral receivables and payables on a net

enforceable master netting agreement exists. U.S. GAAP

significant unobservable inputs, the range of values for 
those inputs and the weighted or arithmetic averages of 
such inputs.  While the determination to classify an 
instrument within level 3 is based on the significance of the 
unobservable inputs to the overall fair value measurement, 
level 3 financial instruments typically include observable 
components (that is, components that are actively quoted 
and can be validated to external sources) in addition to the 
unobservable components. The level 1 and/or level 2 inputs 
are not included in the table. In addition, the  Firm manages 
the risk of the observable components of level 3 financial 
instruments using securities and derivative positions that 
are classified within levels 1 or 2 of the fair value hierarchy.  The range of values presented in the table is representative 
of the highest and lowest level input used to value the 
significant groups of instruments within a product/
instrument classification. Where provided, the weighted 
averages of the input values presented in the table are 
calculated based on the fair value of the instruments that 
the input is being used to value.  
In the  Firm’s view, the input range, weighted and arithmetic 
average values do not reflect the degree of input 
uncertainty or an assessment of the reasonableness of the  
Firm’s estimates and assumptions. Rather, they reflect the 
characteristics of the various instruments held by  the Firm 
and the relative distribution of instruments within the range 
of characteristics. For example, two option contracts may 
have similar levels of market risk exposure and valuation 
uncertainty, but may have significantly different implied 
volatility levels because the option contracts have different 
underlyings, tenors, or strike prices. The input range and 
weighted average values will therefore vary from period-to-
period and parameter-to-parameter based on the 
characteristics of the instruments held by the  Firm at each 
balance sheet date.

  - Commercial mortgage‑backed securities and loans: $0.4B; priced via market comparables.

  - Net interest rate derivatives: $0.4B (option pricing) and $0.0B using discounted cash flows; inputs include interest rate volatilities, spread volatility, interest rate/FX correlations, and prepayment speeds.
  - Net credit derivatives: $0.2B (DCF) and $0.0B (market comparables); inputs include credit correlation, credit spreads, and recovery rates.
  - Net foreign exchange derivatives: $0.3B (option pricing) and a small negative DCF position; inputs include IR‑FX correlation, prepayment speed, and interest rate curve.
  - Net equity derivatives: $(1.2)B; option pricing with forward equity prices, equity volatility, and cross‑asset correlations (equity‑FX, equity‑IR).
  - Net commodity derivatives: $0.0B; option pricing with forward prices (oil and industrial metals), commodity volatility, and correlations.

  - Categories are aggregated by product type and may differ from balance sheet classification; not all listed inputs apply to every instrument.

    - CMBS/loans include nonagency, trading loans, and non‑trading loans.

  - Structured notes within debt/borrowings/deposits contain embedded derivatives; fair value incorporates derivative features with inputs aligned to derivative receivables.
  - Equity securities without readily available quotes are valued using internal techniques (e.g., EBITDA multiples, comparable analysis); all other Level 3 items are individually and in aggregate insignificant.
  - Price input is shown assuming par value of $100; forward equity price is expressed as a percentage of current price.
  - Averages are weighted averages except derivative‑related inputs, which use arithmetic averages.

heading: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
start_phrase: The following tables include a rollforward of the Consolidated balance sheets amounts (including changes in fair value) for financial instruments classified by the Firm within level 3 of the fair value hierarchy for the three and six months ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 .
summary:
- Focus: Disclosure of JPMorgan Chase’s Level 3 fair value measurements (those using significant unobservable inputs), including how changes in unobservable inputs affect fair value and the role of external market factors; references Note 2 of the 2021 Form 10-K for broader methodology and input relationships.

- Scope of rollforward tables: Detailed reconciliations for assets and liabilities classified in Level 3 for:
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021
  These show beginning balances, total realized/unrealized gains/losses, transfers in/out of Level 3, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and ending balances, plus unrealized gains/losses on instruments still held.

- Categories covered:
  - Assets: trading assets (debt instruments such as various mortgage-backed securities, U.S. states/municipal obligations, non-U.S. government and corporate debt, loans, asset-backed securities), equity securities, physical commodities, other; net derivative receivables (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity) presented on a net basis; available-for-sale securities; loans; mortgage servicing rights (MSRs); other assets.
  - Liabilities: deposits, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, accounts payable and other liabilities, long-term debt, and beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs (where applicable).

- Important caveats:
  - Level 3 valuations can include observable components; reported gains/losses include effects from both observable and unobservable inputs.
  - Risk management hedges in Level 1/2 are excluded from the Level 3 tables, so table results do not reflect hedge impacts.

- Reporting locations/footnotes:
  - Most changes run through principal transactions revenue; certain mortgage-related items are in mortgage fees and related income.
  - AFS securities: realized gains/losses in investment securities gains/losses; unrealized in OCI, with amounts disclosed.
  - DVA on fair value option liabilities: realized effects not material; unrealized in OCI, with amounts disclosed.
  - Loan originations included in purchases; settlements include maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, etc.

- Level 3 analysis and key period highlights:
  - Level 3 assets were $22.3 billion at June 30, 2022, up $329 million from March 31, 2022 and up $4.8 billion from December 31, 2021.
  - Primary six-month drivers to June 30, 2022: approximately $1.6 billion increase in gross derivative receivables (gains and purchases, partly offset by transfers) and a $1.9 billion increase in MSRs.

- Transfers between fair value hierarchy levels:
  - Transfers are driven by changes in input observability and/or significance and are assumed to occur at the start of the quarter.
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022: no significant Level 2 to Level 3 transfers; notable Level 3 to Level 2 transfer of interest rate derivative receivables due to increased observability.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022: significant transfers into Level 3 included equity securities (driven by reduced market observability, including restricted access) and equity derivative payables; significant transfers out included interest rate derivative receivables and both equity derivative receivables/payables as observability improved.
  - 2021 comparable periods: no significant Level 2 to Level 3 transfers; notable transfers out of Level 3 included equity derivatives and trading loans as observability improved.

- Proportion of Level 3 to total fair value:
  - Level 3 assets were 2% of total firm assets at fair value at both June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
  - Level 3 liabilities were 8% and 10% of total firm liabilities at fair value at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, respectively.

heading: Consolidated balance sheets changes
start_phrase: The following describes significant changes to level 3 assets since December 31, 2021, for those items measured at fair value on a recurring basis.
summary:
- Clarifies income statement presentation for various fair‑value items:
  - Most fair‑value changes are recorded in principal transactions revenue, except certain CCB mortgage loans, lending‑related commitments intended for sale, and mortgage loan purchase commitments, which are reported in mortgage fees and related income.
  - Available‑for‑sale (AFS) securities: realized gains/losses go to investment securities gains/(losses); unrealized gains/losses go to OCI. No realized gains/losses in income for Q2 or YTD June 30 in 2022 or 2021. Unrealized OCI impact: $(19) million (Q2’22) vs $0 (Q2’21); $8 million (6M’22) vs $0 (6M’21).
  - Mortgage servicing rights (MSRs): fair‑value changes are reported in mortgage fees and related income.
  - Debit valuation adjustment (DVA) on fair value option liabilities: realized effects in principal transactions revenue (not material for Q2 and 6M in 2022 and 2021); unrealized effects in OCI of $(344) million (Q2’22) vs $5 million (Q2’21) and $(574) million (6M’22) vs $(17) million (6M’21).
  - Loan originations are included in purchases.
  - Other activity includes maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, and miscellaneous items.

- Level 3 fair value analysis (recurring basis):
  - Level 3 assets were $22.3 billion at June 30, 2022, up $329 million from March 31, 2022 and up $4.8 billion from December 31, 2021.
  - Six‑month increase drivers: +$1.6 billion in gross derivative receivables (gains and purchases, largely offset by net transfers) and +$1.9 billion in MSRs.
  - Transfers for Q2 2022:
    - No significant transfers from Level 2 to Level 3.
    - Level 3 to Level 2: $930 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables due to increased observability and lower significance of unobservable inputs.
  - Transfers for six months ended June 30, 2022:
    - Level 2 to Level 3: $1.6 billion of total debt and equity instruments (including $959 million of equity securities) due to decreased observability/restricted market access; $1.3 billion of gross equity derivative payables due to decreased observability and greater reliance on unobservable inputs.
    - Level 3 to Level 2: $965 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables; $920 million of gross equity derivative receivables; $1.4 billion of gross equity derivative payables, all due to increased observability and reduced unobservable input significance.
  - Comparative 2021 transfers:
    - No significant Level 2 to Level 3 transfers for Q2 or 6M 2021.
    - Level 3 to Level 2: $1.0 billion of gross equity derivative receivables (Q2’21); for 6M’21, $800 million of total debt and equity instruments (largely trading loans), $1.3 billion of gross equity derivative receivables, and $1.1 billion of gross equity derivative payables, driven by increased observability.
  - All transfers are based on changes in the observability or significance of valuation inputs and are assumed to occur at the start of the reporting quarter.

- H1 2021 results:

text:
Equity securities without readily determinable fair values 
The Firm measures certain equity securities without readily determinable fair values at cost less impairment (if any), plus or 
minus observable price changes from an identical or similar investment of the same issuer (i.e., measurement alternative), 
with such changes recognized in other income.  
In its determination of the new carrying values upon observable price changes,  the Firm may adjust the prices if deemed 
necessary to arrive at  the Firm’s estimated fair values. Such adjustments may include adjustments to reflect the different 
rights and obligations of similar securities, and other adjustments that are consistent with  the Firm’s valuation techniques for 
private equity direct investments.

title: Fair value option - Introduction
heading: Note 3 – Fair value option
start_phrase: The fair value option provides an option to elect fair value for selected financial assets, fina ncial liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
summary: Overview of the Firm’s fair value option (FVO) policy and scope: the Firm may elect fair value measurement for certain financial assets, liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments to mitigate income statement volatility from mixed measurement bases and to reflect instruments managed on a fair value basis. Elections include loans purchased or originated for securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation, or otherwise managed at fair value (including lending-related commitments); certain securities financing agreements; owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets with embedded credit derivatives that would otherwise require separate derivative accounting; structured notes and other hybrid instruments with embedded derivatives issued or transacted in client-driven activities; and certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts when underlying assets are at fair value.
text:
Fair value option 
The fair value option provides an option to elect fair value  for selected financial assets, fina ncial liabilities, unrecognized firm 
commitments, and written loan commitments.  
The Firm has elected to measure certain instruments at fair value for several reasons including to mitigate income statement 
volatility caused by the differences between the measurement basis of elected instruments (e.g., certain instruments that 
otherwise would be accounted for on an accrual basis) and the associated risk management arrangements that are accounted 
for on a fair value basis, as well as to better reflect those instruments that are managed on a fair value basis.  
The Firm’s election of fair value includes the following instruments:  
•Loans purchased or originated as part of securitization warehousing activity, subject to bifurcation accounting, or managed 
on a fair value basis, including lending-related commitments  
•Certain securities financing agreements  
•Owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets that contain embedded credit derivatives, which would otherwise 
be required to be separately accounted for as a derivative instrument  
•Structured notes and other hybrid instruments, which are predominantly financial instruments that contain embedded 
derivatives, that are issued or transacted as part of client-driven activities  
•Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by  CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts where the underlying assets are 
carried at fair value

The primary reasons are to reduce income statement volatility arising from mixed measurement bases and to align accounting with instruments managed on a fair value basis.

- Instruments elected for fair value:
  - Loans tied to securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation, or otherwise managed on a fair value basis (including lending-related commitments).
  - Certain securities financing agreements.
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized assets that contain embedded credit derivatives (avoiding separate derivative accounting).
  - Structured notes and other hybrid instruments (primarily with embedded derivatives) issued or transacted in client-driven activities.
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB consolidated securitization trusts where underlying assets are at fair value.

- Results presented: A table of changes in fair value recognized in the Consolidated statements of income for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, split between principal transactions and all other income, and by instrument category. Related risk management instruments (which are at fair value) are excluded from the table.

- Key performance highlights:
  - 2022 saw sizable gains in long-term debt measured at fair value (predominantly structured notes): approximately $5.4B in Q2 and $9.4B YTD, versus losses in 2021.

  - Federal funds sold/securities purchased under resale and securities borrowed showed losses in 2022.
  - Minimal activity for beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs.

- Presentation and accounting details:
  - For liabilities under the fair value option, unrealized gains/losses from instrument-specific credit risk (DVA) are recorded in OCI; realized DVA is recorded in principal transactions (realized amounts were not material for Q2 and were small YTD in both years).

title: Derivative instruments - Introduction
heading: Note 4 – Derivative instruments
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase makes markets in derivatives for clients and also uses derivatives to hedge or manage its own risk exposures.
summary: Introduces JPMorgan Chase’s use of derivatives for client market-making and for hedging/managing its own risks, with disclosures organized by accounting treatment and purpose per Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K. Only a limited number are designated in hedge accounting relationships—fair value, cash flow, or net investment hedges—covering interest rate (fixed-rate and floating-rate exposures), foreign exchange (assets/liabilities, forecasted revenue/expense, and net investments), and commodity inventory, primarily in Corporate and, for commodities, CIB and AWM. Non-designated derivatives include “specified risk management” for interest rate risks tied to mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, and MSRs (CCB), credit risk of wholesale lending (CIB), and certain other interest rate/FX risks (Corporate). Market-making and other activities use various derivatives in CIB, with additional “other derivatives” across CIB, AWM, and Corporate. A table maps these uses to hedge designations, affected segments (Corporate, CIB, AWM, CCB), and related 10-Q page references (119–123).

- Topic: Disclosure of derivatives netting, collateral, and resulting exposures.
- Scope and dates: Presents, in millions, gross and net derivative receivables and payables by contract type and settlement type as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Netting methodology: Derivative positions and related cash collateral are netted on the Consolidated balance sheets only when governed by a master netting agreement supported by an appropriate legal opinion; otherwise they are shown separately and are not eligible for GAAP netting.
- Collateral treatment:
  - Cash collateral related to OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives is included in amounts netted on the balance sheets.
  - Additional collateral (liquid securities and other cash held at third‑party custodians) mitigates counterparty credit risk but is not eligible for net presentation; it is disclosed as “Collateral not nettable on the Consolidated balance sheets,” limited to the fair value exposure to each counterparty.
  - Excess collateral over exposure and collateral tied to agreements lacking appropriate legal opinions are excluded from the collateral totals shown.
  - “Liquid securities” align with high-quality liquid assets under the LCR rule.
- Product and settlement breakdown: Detailed tables for interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity contracts, split into OTC, OTC‑cleared, and exchange‑traded categories, showing gross amounts, amounts netted, and resulting net receivables/payables.
- Legal opinion status: Totals distinguish between derivatives with appropriate legal opinions (eligible for GAAP netting) and those without (reported gross and not netted), for both receivables and payables.
- Consolidated totals: Provides total derivative receivables and payables recognized on the balance sheets, followed by “Collateral not nettable” and resulting net amounts after considering such collateral.
- Footnotes/highlights:
  - Exchange‑traded futures are settled daily.
  - Collateral disclosure relates only to OTC and OTC‑cleared derivatives.
  - For some counterparties, reported third‑party collateral is capped at the net derivative balance.
  - Discloses the cash collateral amounts included in netted positions at each date (for both net derivatives receivable and payable).

heading: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
start_phrase: Refer to Note 5 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features related to the Firm’s derivative contracts.
summary:
- Focus: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features associated with JPMorgan Chase’s OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives, including downgrade-triggered collateral and termination provisions; reference to Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K for broader context.
- Net derivative payables and collateral (in millions):
  - June 30, 2022: net derivative payables $16,037; collateral posted $14,926.
  - December 31, 2021: net derivative payables $20,114; collateral posted $19,402.
- Ratings downgrade impact on liquidity for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and subsidiaries (predominantly JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.):
  - Additional collateral required (in millions):
    - Single-notch: $273 (6/30/22) vs. $219 (12/31/21)
    - Two-notch: $1,552 (6/30/22) vs. $1,577 (12/31/21)
  - Termination payment amounts (fair values of payables; exclude collateral) (in millions):
    - Single-notch: $85 (6/30/22) vs. $98 (12/31/21)
    - Two-notch: $700 (6/30/22) vs. $787 (12/31/21)
- Mechanics/assumptions:
  - Downgrade triggers require collateral posting or contract termination when predefined rating thresholds are breached.
  - A downgrade by a single agency that does not fall below a corresponding rating from another major agency generally does not trigger additional collateral or termination, except in certain cases where additional initial margin may be required.
  - Liquidity impact is calculated assuming a downgrade below the lowest current rating referenced in each contract.
- Derivatives executed in contemplation of asset sales:
  - The Firm sometimes transfers financial assets while retaining economic exposure via a derivative with the same counterparty.
  - Generally accounted for as collateralized financings (see Note 10); in limited cases, accounted for as a sale plus a derivative under U.S. GAAP.
  - Amounts outstanding under such sales-with-derivative structures were not material at June 30, 2022, and December 31, 2021.

summary:
- Focus: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income, specifically fair value hedge accounting.
- Content of tables: Pre-tax gains/losses on derivatives and related hedged items by contract type (interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Presentation details:
  - Gains/losses on hedging derivatives are reported in the same income statement line as the hedged items.
  - Income statement impacts shown include: (1) derivative and hedged item effects, (2) the impact of excluded components via amortization and current-period fair value changes, and (3) related OCI impact for excluded components.
- Contract-type specifics:
  - Interest rate hedges: Benchmark rate risk (e.g., LIBOR, SOFR) of fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded in net interest income. From Jan 1, 2022, presentation includes amortization of the inception hedge accounting adjustment; prior periods revised. Interest accruals on swaps and related hedged items are excluded.
  - Foreign exchange hedges: Spot FX risk of long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges: Overall fair value hedges of physical commodities inventories; impacts recorded in principal transactions revenue.
- Excluded components policy: Certain elements (e.g., forward points, time value, cross-currency basis spreads) are excluded from effectiveness assessment and affect earnings either through amortization over the derivative’s life or through current-period fair value changes; changes in excluded amounts under the amortization approach are recorded in OCI and amortized to earnings.
- Prior-period revisions: Select 2021 amounts revised to conform to the current presentation.
- Balance sheet disclosures (June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Carrying amounts of hedged AFS securities, long-term debt, and beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs, and the cumulative fair value hedge basis adjustments embedded in those carrying amounts, shown separately for active and discontinued hedging relationships.
  - These cumulative basis adjustments are expected to reverse through future net interest income as yield adjustments; sign conventions indicate whether they will increase or reduce NII.
  - Exclusions: Physical commodities inventories measured at fair value under hedge accounting (no incremental future net income impact), and items hedged solely for FX risk (basis adjustments do not reverse through earnings). Carrying amount for AFS is at amortized cost, net of allowance.

heading: Credit derivatives
start_phrase: Refer to Note 5 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of credit derivatives.
summary:
- Scope: Extract from JPMorgan Chase’s financial notes covering credit derivatives exposure/details and components of noninterest revenue for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 (with prior-year comparisons) and positions as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Credit derivatives overview:
  - Notional amounts are not the Firm’s primary risk metric because they ignore credit event probability, recoveries, and hedges.
  - Summary of gross protection sold and purchased by product:
    - Credit default swaps and other credit derivatives (e.g., credit swap options, total return swaps), plus credit-related notes.
    - As of June 30, 2022: $526.1B protection sold; $551.6B protection purchased with identical underlyings; net protection purchased of $25.5B; $28.4B of other protection purchased (incl. $9.0B credit-related notes).
    - As of December 31, 2021: $499.6B protection sold; $537.8B purchased with identical underlyings; net protection purchased of $38.2B; $25.1B other protection purchased (incl. $9.4B credit-related notes).
  - Protection sold ratings/maturity profile (seller of protection only):
    - Breakout by investment-grade vs noninvestment-grade and by remaining maturity buckets (<1 year, 1–5 years, >5 years).
    - Fair value shown gross (pre-netting/collateral): June 30, 2022 net fair value liability of $5.1B vs net asset of $3.6B at December 31, 2021.
    - Ratings based on S&P/Moody’s; maturity based on contractual remaining term.
  - Clarifying footnotes: definition of “identical underlyings,” settlement values exclude reference obligation fair value at settlement, and “other protection purchased” represents positions without an offsetting identical sold position.
- Noninterest revenue (Note 5) components and trends:
  - Investment banking fees:

summary:
- Focus: Summary tables and notes on card income, certain noninterest expenses, and detailed interest income/expense for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021 (JPMorgan Chase).

- Card income:
  - Components shown: interchange and merchant processing income; rewards costs and partner payments; other card income.
  - Other card income primarily reflects amortization of account origination costs and annual fees.
  - Totals declined year over year: Q2 2022 $1,133mm vs. $1,647mm; 1H 2022 $2,108mm vs. $2,997mm, as higher rewards/partner payments and negative other card income more than offset higher interchange/merchant processing income.
  - Cross-references: Note 14 (mortgage fees and related income) and Note 16 (operating lease income within other income).

- Noninterest expense – Other expense:
  - Legal expense disclosed: lower year over year (Q2 2022 $73mm vs. $185mm; 1H 2022 $192mm vs. $213mm).

- Note 6 – Interest income and interest expense:
  - Refers to 2021 Form 10-K Note 7 for accounting policies.
  - Detailed breakdowns provided for interest income (loans; taxable and non-taxable securities; trading assets – debt instruments; federal funds/resale agreements; securities borrowed; deposits with banks; all other interest-earning assets) and interest expense (interest-bearing deposits; repos; short-term borrowings; trading liabilities and other interest-bearing liabilities; long-term debt; beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs).
  - Totals and performance:
    - Total interest income increased (Q2 2022 $18,646mm vs. $14,094mm; 1H 2022 $34,142mm vs. $28,365mm).
    - Total interest expense rose significantly (Q2 2022 $3,518mm vs. $1,353mm; 1H 2022 $5,142mm vs. $2,735mm).
    - Net interest income up year over year (Q2 2022 $15,128mm vs. $12,741mm; 1H 2022 $29,000mm vs. $25,630mm).
    - Provision for credit losses shifted to an expense from a prior-year benefit (Q2 2022 $1,101mm vs. $(2,285)mm; 1H 2022 $2,564mm vs. $(6,441)mm), resulting in lower net interest income after provision (Q2 2022 $14,027mm vs. $15,026mm; 1H 2022 $26,436mm vs. $32,071mm).
  - Footnotes clarify: inclusion of amortization/accretion of unearned income; tax-exempt securities; mechanics of negative interest on securities borrowed and certain trading liabilities; classification of brokerage-related receivables in other assets; inclusion of commercial paper in short-term borrowings; and inclusion of interest on brokerage-related customer payables in other interest-bearing liabilities.

Taxable-equivalent amounts are used where applicable. The effective yield excludes unscheduled principal prepayments; and accordingly, actual 
maturities of securities may differ from their contractual or expected maturities as certain securities may be prepaid. However, for certain callable debt 
securities, the average yield is calculated to the earliest call date.
(b)Substantially all of the Firm’s U.S. residential MBS and collateralized mortgage obligations are due in 10 years  or more, based on contractual maturity. The 
estimated weighted-average life, which reflects anticipated future prepayments, is approximately eight years  for agency residential MBS, seven years  for 
agency residential collateralized mortgage obligations and six years  for nonagency residential collateralized mortgage obligations.

summary:
- Scope: Excerpt details securities financing agreements (repos and securities lending), related collateral types and maturities, transfers that failed sale accounting, and loan accounting/portfolio composition with balances as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

- Securities financing agreements – collateral types and balances:
  - Presents gross liability balances by collateral type for:

- Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting:
  - Assets with transferred rights that failed sale accounting under U.S. GAAP recognized as collateralized financings.
  - Balances held: $342M at June 30, 2022; $440M at December 31, 2021.

- Loan accounting framework:

title: Loan accounting framework
heading: Loan accounting framework
start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
summary:
- Outlines the loan accounting framework, which depends on management’s strategy, with three categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value.
- Provides cross-references for detailed policies and disclosures: Note 12 of the 2021 Form 10-K for loan accounting policies; Note 3 of this Form 10-Q for fair value option elections; Note 2 of this Form 10-Q for loans at fair value classified as trading assets.
- Describes the loan portfolio segmentation used for the allowance for loan losses: three segments—Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale—and the loan classes within each:

Notes that wholesale classifications align with bank regulatory agencies and include certain risk-rated loans in CCB; references Note 14 of the 2021 Form 10-K for SPEs.

  - Retained loans rose across segments; held-for-sale balances declined; fair value balances shifted (notably lower in Consumer, excluding credit card).

Loan accounting framework
The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.  The Firm accounts for loans based on the following 
categories:
•Originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (i.e., “retained”)
•Loans held-for-sale
•Loans at fair value
Refer to Note  12 of JPMorgan Chase's 2021 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion of loans, including accounting policies. Refer 
to Note  3 of this Form 10-Q for further information on  the Firm's elections of fair value accounting under the fair value option. 
Refer to Note  2 of this Form 10-Q for information on loans carried at fair value and classified as trading assets.

- Accounting framework:
  - Loans are accounted for as (i) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), (ii) loans held-for-sale (HFS), or (iii) loans at fair value.
  - Cross-references: Note 12 (2021 Form 10-K) for detailed loan accounting policies; Note 3 (current 10-Q) for fair value option elections; Note 2 (current 10-Q) for loans at fair value classified as trading assets.

- Portfolio segmentation and classes used for allowance determination:

  - Classes:

    - Credit card: Credit card loans.
    - Wholesale: Secured by real estate; Commercial and industrial; Other.
  - Clarifications:
    - Residential real estate includes scored mortgage and home equity loans in CCB and AWM, and scored mortgage loans in CIB and Corporate.
    - Wholesale segment includes loans across CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate, and certain risk-rated CCB loans; classes align with bank regulatory classifications.
    - “Other” includes loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies/trusts, and individuals (predominantly AWM Global Private Bank clients). Reference to Note 14 (2021 Form 10-K) for SPEs.

summary:
- Describes how residential real estate loan modifications are treated as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs) when the Firm grants concessions to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty; short-term or insignificant modifications are not TDRs.
- Reports carrying value of new TDRs: $115 million (Q2 2022) vs $307 million (Q2 2021); $233 million (H1 2022) vs $558 million (H1 2021). No additional lending commitments to borrowers with TDR-modified residential loans.
- Explains nature of concessions under the Firm’s and government (including U.S. GSE) programs: interest rate reductions; term or payment extensions; delays/deferrals of principal and/or interest; principal forgiveness; and “other” items such as converting variable to fixed rates and payment delays that meet the TDR definition.
- Activity metrics:
  - Trial modifications approved: 1,165 (Q2 2022) vs 1,165 (Q2 2021); 2,691 (H1 2022) vs 2,566 (H1 2021).
  - Permanent modifications: 1,289 (Q2 2022) vs 1,186 (Q2 2021); 2,831 (H1 2022) vs 2,900 (H1 2021).
- Mix of concessions among permanent modifications (percent of loans; totals exceed 100% as most loans receive multiple concessions; trial mod concessions generally align with permanent):
  - Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021: interest rate reduction 45% vs 78%; term/payment extension 54% vs 51%; principal/interest deferred 10% vs 18%; principal forgiveness 1% vs 0%; other 46% vs 34%.
  - H1 2022 vs H1 2021: interest rate reduction 56% vs 74%; term/payment extension 67% vs 45%; principal/interest deferred 12% vs 26%; principal forgiveness 1% vs 2%; other 36% vs 44%.
- Notes exclusions: Chapter 7 loans where the only concession is debt discharge and loans with short-term or otherwise insignificant non-concession modifications.

title: Loan modifications
heading: Loan modifications
start_phrase:
The Firm may offer loan modification programs granting 
concessions to credit card borrowers who are experiencing 
financial difficulty.
summary:
- The firm offers long-term loan modification programs to credit card borrowers in financial difficulty, typically structured as fixed payment plans of about 60 months with reduced interest rates; substantially all such long-term modifications are classified as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs), while short-term or insignificant non-concession changes are not TDRs.
- If borrowers fail to comply with modified terms, loans continue to age and are ultimately charged off under the firm’s standard charge-off policy; in most cases, the borrower’s credit line is not reinstated.
- Financial effects and activity levels: new TDR enrollments were less than 1% of total retained credit card loans for all periods presented.
- Balances of new TDRs: $81 million (Q2 2022) vs $90 million (Q2 2021); $163 million (H1 2022) vs $233 million (H1 2021).
- Interest rate reductions: weighted-average APR before vs after TDR—Q2 2022: 18.94% to 4.62%; Q2 2021: 17.92% to 5.15%; H1 2022: 18.47% to 4.75%; H1 2021: 17.81% to 5.20%.
- Redeaults within one year of modification: $8 million (Q2 2022) vs $13 million (Q2 2021); $17 million (H1 2022) vs $32 million (H1 2021).
- Payment default for modified credit card loans is defined as missing two consecutive contractual payments; defaulted modified loans remain in the program and are charged off per standard policy.
- Footnotes clarify that new TDR balances represent outstanding balances prior to modification and that redefault amounts reflect balances at quarter-end of the default.
text:
Loan modifications
The Firm may offer loan modification programs granting 
concessions to credit card borrowers who are experiencing 
financial difficulty. The  Firm grants concessions for most of 
the credit card loans under long-term programs. These 
modifications involve placing the customer on a fixed 
payment plan, generally for  60 months, and typically 
include reducing the interest rate on the credit card. 
Substantially all modifications under the  Firm’s long-term 
programs are considered to be TDRs. Loans with short-term 
or other insignificant modifications that are not considered 
concessions are not TDRs.  
If the cardholder does not comply with the modified 
payment terms, then the credit card loan continues to age 
and will ultimately be charged-off in accordance with  the 
Firm’s standard charge-off policy. In most cases,  the Firm 
does not reinstate the borrower’s line of credit.

  - New TDR enrollments were less than 1% of total retained credit card loans in all disclosed periods.

Loan modifications
Certain loan modifications are considered to be TDRs as they provide various concessions to borrowers who are experiencing 
financial difficulty. Loans with short-term or other insignificant modifications that are not considered concessions are not 
TDRs.  New TDRs were $60 million  and $224 million  for the three months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, and 2021 , respectively and

and Industrial loan class.  New TDRs for the six months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021  reflected modifications that included 
extending maturity dates and covenant waivers for both periods as well as the receipt of assets in partial satisfaction of the 
loan in 2021 predominantly in the Commercial and Industrial loan class . The impact of these modifications resulting in new 
TDRs was not material to  the Firm for the  three and six months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021 .

Includes loan loss allowances, lending-related commitments, and investment securities allowances, plus collateral-dependent loan data and footnotes.

- Allowance for loan losses (rollforward):
  - Ending balance: $17.75B in 2022 vs. $19.50B in 2021.
  - Net charge-offs/(recoveries): $1.239B in 2022 vs. $1.791B in 2021.
  - Provision for loan losses: $2.598B build in 2022 vs. $(7.038)B release in 2021.
  - Segment notes: Credit card allowance declined ($10.4B vs. $12.5B); wholesale increased ($5.421B vs. $5.102B); consumer ex-CC slightly higher ($1.929B vs. $1.898B).

- Allowance for lending-related commitments (rollforward):
  - Ending balance: $2.222B in 2022 vs. $2.998B in 2021.
  - Provision: $(39)M in 2022 vs. $588M in 2021.

- Total allowance for credit losses (loans + lending commitments + securities):
  - $20.019B in 2022 vs. $22.585B in 2021.
  - Investment securities allowance: $47M in 2022 vs. $87M in 2021.

- Impairment methodology detail:
  - Allowance for loan losses:
    - Asset-specific: $(117)M total in 2022 vs. $374M in 2021 (segment mix shows negative in consumer ex-CC, positive in credit card and wholesale).
    - Portfolio-based: $17.867B in 2022 vs. $19.126B in 2021.
  - Loans by methodology:
    - Total retained loans: $1.052T in 2022 vs. $0.964T in 2021; predominantly portfolio-based ($1.036T in 2022).
  - Lending-related commitments allowance:
    - Asset-specific: $78M in 2022 vs. $150M in 2021.

  - Asset-specific includes collateral-dependent loans, TDRs (or expected TDRs), modified PCD loans, and certain nonaccrual wholesale loans; credit card asset-specific TDR allowance uses original contractual rates.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities.

- Overall themes:
  - Year-over-year decline in total allowance for credit losses driven by lower credit card and commitment allowances.
  - 2022 shows a reserve build versus large reserve releases in 2021.
  - Portfolio-based methodology remains the dominant driver of allowances and balances.

start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 was $20.0 billion , an increas e of $ 1 . 3 b i l l i o n from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, consisting of: $1.0 billion in wholesale and $311 million in consumer.
summary:
- Allowance for credit losses (ACL) was $20.0B at June 30, 2022, up $1.3B from December 31, 2021, driven by a $1.0B increase in wholesale and $311M in consumer.
- Key drivers of the increase: higher weighting of adverse scenarios tied to inflation, monetary policy changes, and geopolitical risks (including the war in Ukraine); modest deterioration in the firm’s macroeconomic outlook; loan growth in Card and Commercial Banking in 2Q22; and client-specific Russia/Russia-associated downgrades in CIB and AWM in 1Q22.
- ACL is estimated using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios; adverse scenarios assume more punitive conditions than the central case, resulting in weighted-average U.S. unemployment above 4% through 4Q23 and a U.S. real GDP level 1.1% lower by 4Q23.
- Central case assumptions (as of June 30, 2022): U.S. unemployment 3.6% (4Q22), 3.6% (2Q23), 3.7% (4Q23); YoY U.S. real GDP growth 1.3%, 1.7%, 1.2%. Prior assumptions (as of December 31, 2021): unemployment 4.2% (2Q22), 4.0% (4Q22), 3.9% (2Q23); YoY GDP growth 3.1%, 2.8%, 2.1%.
- Future changes to forecasts will be reflected in the provision for credit losses.
- References provided to Notes and sections for detailed policies, portfolio information, and critical accounting estimates.

Discussion of changes in the allowance
The allowance for credit losses as of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2 was 
$20.0 billion , an increas e of $ 1 . 3  b i l l i o n from 
D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, consisting of: $1.0 billion  in wholesale  
and $311 million  in consumer.
The change in allowance  reflect s the increased weight 
placed on the adverse scenarios in the current year, du e to 
the ongoing effects associated with higher inflation , 
changes in monetary policy, and geopolitical risks, including 
the war in Ukraine, and a modest deterioration in the Firm's 
macroeconomic forecast.  The increase in the allowance was 
also driven by loan growth in Card and CB in the second 
quarter of 2022, and client-specific Russia and Russia-
associated downgrades in CIB a nd AWM in the first quarter 
of 2022.
The Firm's allowance for credit losses is estimated using a 
weighted average of five internally developed 
macroeconomic scenarios. The adverse scenarios 
incorporate more punitive macroeconomic factors than the 
central case assumptions provided in the table below, 
resulting in weighted average U.S. unemployment rates 
above 4% through the fourth quarter of 2023, and a 1.1% 
lower U.S. real GDP level exiting the fourth quarter of 2023.The Firm’s central case assumptions reflected U.S. 
unemployment rates and U.S. real GDP as follows:

title: Variable interest entities - Introduction
heading: Note 13 – Variable interest entities
start_phrase: Refer to Note 1 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a further description of JPMorgan Chase’s accounting policies regarding consolidation of VIEs.
summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s variable interest entities (VIEs), with references to Note 1 of the 2021 Form 10-K for consolidation accounting policies and Note 14 for VIEs and securitizations. Defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs as those where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets, the VIE issues instruments bearing the JPMorgan Chase name, or it is a JPMorgan Chase–administered asset‑backed commercial paper conduit. Summarizes significant Firm‑sponsored VIE types by business segment with Form 10‑Q page references: in CCB, credit card securitization trusts (securitizing originated credit card receivables) and mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitizing originated and purchased residential mortgages) (pp. 152–154); in CIB, mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans) (pp. 152–154), multi‑seller conduits (client access to markets and transaction structuring) (p. 154), and municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments) (p. 154). Notes the Firm also invests in and provides financing and services to third‑party‑sponsored VIEs, with consolidated VIE assets and liabilities and third‑party VIE details on pages 155–157.

Variable interest entities
Refer to Note  1 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K  for a further description of  JPMorgan Chase’s accounting policies 
regarding consolidation of VIEs.  Refer to Note  14 of JPMorgan Chase's 2021 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion of VIEs, 
including  the Firm’s accounting policies regarding securitizations.
The following table summarizes the most significant types of  Firm- sponsored VIEs by business  segment. The Firm considers a 
“Firm-sponsored” VIE to include any entity where: (1) JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary of the structure; (2) the VIE 
is used by JPMorgan Chase to securitize Firm assets; (3) the VIE issues financial instruments with the JPMorgan Chase name; or 
(4) the entity is a JPMorgan Chase–administered asset-backed commercial paper conduit.

summary:

title: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
heading: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
start_phrase: The Firm securitizes (or has securitized) originated and purchased residential mortgages, commercial mortgages and other consumer loans primarily in its CCB and CIB businesses.
summary:
- Focus: Note 13 covers JPMorgan Chase’s involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs), referencing the 2021 Form 10-K for consolidation and securitization accounting policies (Notes 1 and 14).
- Definition of Firm‑sponsored VIEs: Includes entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary; uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets; the VIE issues instruments bearing the JPMorgan Chase name; or the VIE is a Firm‑administered ABCP conduit.
- Types by business segment (with page references): 
  - CCB: Credit card securitization trusts (securitization of originated card receivables; p.152); mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages; pp.152–154).
  - CIB: Mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial mortgages, and other consumer loans; pp.152–154); multi‑seller conduits (client funding/access to markets; p.154); municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments; p.154).
- Third‑party VIEs: The Firm also invests in, finances, and provides services to VIEs sponsored by others; see pp.155–157 for consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and third‑party‑sponsored VIE details.
- Significant Firm‑sponsored VIEs:
  - Credit card securitizations: The Firm is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust due to continuing involvement.
  - Mortgage and other securitization trusts: The Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans (primarily in CCB and CIB), may act as servicer, and may retain beneficial interests.
- Continuing involvement and risk: Continuing involvement includes servicing, retained senior/subordinated interests (including risk‑retention), recourse/guarantees, and derivatives; in some cases involvement is only servicing. Maximum loss exposure on retained/purchased interests equals their carrying value.
- Quantitative disclosures for Firm‑sponsored private‑label securitizations (excludes GSE/agency):
  - June 30, 2022: Total assets in securitization VIEs $231.3B; consolidated VIE assets $0.8B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement $172.2B; JPMorgan interests in nonconsolidated VIEs $9.1B (primarily investment securities) across prime/Alt‑A, subprime, and commercial/other.
  - December 31, 2021: Total assets $216.7B; consolidated $1.0B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement $150.8B; JPMorgan interests $6.2B.
- Credit quality of retained interests: 86% (June 30, 2022) and 79% (December 31, 2021) rated A or better (S&P‑equivalent); investment‑grade vs. non‑investment‑grade amounts disclosed for prime residential and commercial/other retained interests.
- Footnote highlights: Excludes GSE/agency securitizations, retained servicing, and certain derivatives; “commercial and other” includes CRE‑backed and non‑mortgage consumer receivables purchased from third parties; includes re‑securitizations; excludes certain market‑making positions.

title: Residential mortgage
heading: Residential mortgage
start_phrase: The Firm securitizes residential mortgage loans originated by CCB, as well as residential mortgage loans purchased from third parties by either CCB or CIB.
summary:
- The Firm’s securitization activities include:
  - Residential mortgages: Securitizes loans originated by CCB and loans purchased from third parties by CCB or CIB.
  - Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations: CIB originates and securitizes commercial mortgage loans and underwrites/trades securities issued by securitization trusts.

- Re-securitizations:
  - Transfers to re-securitization VIEs of U.S. GSE and government agency securities totaled $7.373B (Q2 2022) vs $18.794B (Q2 2021); $13.449B (H1 2022) vs $31.899B (H1 2021).
  - No transfers of private-label securities during the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021; retained interests in any Firm-sponsored VIEs were not material as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
  - Interests in nonconsolidated U.S. GSE/government agency re-securitization VIEs were $2.470B at June 30, 2022 vs $1.947B at December 31, 2021.
  - The Firm did not consolidate any U.S. GSE/government agency or Firm-sponsored private-label re-securitization VIEs as of those dates.

- Multi-seller conduits:
  - The Firm makes markets in and invests in commercial paper issued by Firm-administered conduits; holdings were $12.1B (June 30, 2022) and $13.7B (December 31, 2021), eliminated in consolidation.
  - Investments reflect funding needs/capacity, not market illiquidity; no obligation to purchase conduit commercial paper beyond credit risk retention requirements.
  - Deal-specific and program-wide liquidity facilities and credit enhancement provided by the Firm are eliminated in consolidation.
  - The Firm or its conduits provide lending-related commitments to certain clients; unfunded commitments were $13.1B (June 30, 2022) and $13.4B (December 31, 2021), reported off-balance sheet (see Note 22).

- Municipal bond vehicles:
  - TOB (tender option bond) trusts facilitate financing municipal bond investments at short-term rates.
  - Customer TOB trusts are sponsored by third parties; the Firm sponsors all non-customer TOB transactions.

text:
Multi-seller conduits
In the normal course of business,  JPMorgan Chase makes 
markets in and invests in commercial paper issued by  the 
Firm -administered multi-seller conduits.  The Firm held 
$12.1 billion  and $13.7 billion  of the commercial paper 
issued by  the Firm -administered multi-seller conduits at  
J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, respectively,  
which have been eliminated in consolidation.  The Firm’s 
investments reflect  the Firm’s funding needs and capacity 
and were not driven by market illiquidity.  Other than the 
amounts required to be held pursuant to credit risk 
retention rules,  the Firm is not obligated under any 
agreement to purchase the commercial paper issued by  the 
Firm -administered multi-seller conduits.
Deal-specific liquidity facilities, program-wide liquidity and 
credit enhancement provided by the Firm have been 
eliminated in consolidation. The Firm or the Firm-
administered multi-seller conduits provide lending-related 
commitments to certain clients of the Firm-administered 
multi-seller conduits. The unfunded commitments were  
$13.1 billion  and $13.4 billion  at J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, and 
D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, respectively,  and are reported as off-
balance sheet lending-related commitments in other 
unfunded commitments to extend credit. Refer to Note  22 
for more information on off-balance sheet lending-related 
commitments.

text:
VIEs sponsored by third parties
The Firm enters into transactions with VIEs structured by 
other parties. These include, for example, acting as a 
derivative counterparty, liquidity provider , investor , 
underwriter, placement agent, remarketing agent, trustee 
or custodian. These transactions are conducted at arm’s-
length, and individual credit decisions are based on the 
analysis of the specific VIE, taking into consideration the 
quality of the underlying assets. Where  the Firm does not 
have the power to direct the activities of the VIE that most 
significantly impact the VIE’s economic performance, or a 
variable interest that could potentially be significant,  the 
Firm generally does not consolidate the VIE, but it records 
and reports these positions on its Consolidated balance 
sheets in the same manner it would record and report 
positions in respect of any other third-party transaction.

Tax credit vehicles 
The Firm  holds investments in unconsolidated tax credit 
vehicles, which are limited partnerships and similar entities 
that own and operate affordable housing , energy, and other  
projects. These entities are primarily considered VIEs. A 
third party is typically the general partner or managing member and has control over the significant activities of the 
tax credit vehicles, and accordingly  the Firm does not 
consolidate tax credit vehicles.  The Firm generally invests in 
these partnerships as a limited partner and earns a return 
primarily through the receipt of tax credits allocated to the 
projects. The maximum loss exposure, represented by 
equity investments and funding commitments, was  $27.5

billion  was unfunded at  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2 and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  
2021 , respectively.  The Firm assesses each project and to 
reduce the risk of loss, may withhold varying amounts of its 
capital investment until the project qualifies for tax credits. 
Refer to Note  25 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 10-K for 
further information on affordable housing tax credits  and 
Note 22 of this Form 10-Q for more information on off-

- Loan securitizations:

    - Principal securitized: Q2 2022 $3.0B (residential) and $4.0B (commercial/other); Q2 2021 $4.1B and $2.9B; 1H 2022 $9.5B and $7.1B; 1H 2021 $8.2B and $4.8B.
    - Cash flows during the periods include proceeds from loan sales (predominantly Level 2 financial instruments), servicing fees, and interest cash flows; carrying value of loans at fair value approximated sale proceeds.
    - Residential amounts represent prime mortgages; excludes GSE/government agency securitizations; commercial/other includes commercial mortgages and other consumer loans; re-securitizations are excluded.

- Sales to U.S. GSEs and Ginnie Mae:
  - The Firm sells originated and purchased mortgage loans and certain originated excess MSRs on a nonrecourse basis primarily to GSEs for securitization with GSE guarantees, and into Ginnie Mae securitizations typically insured/guaranteed by U.S. government agencies.
  - The Firm does not consolidate the related securitization vehicles as it is not the primary beneficiary.
  - For a limited number of sales, the Firm shares a portion of the credit risk; references are made to other notes for indemnification details and the impact of excess MSR sales.

The Firm may provide various services to customer TOB 
trusts, including  remarketing agent, liquidity or tender 
option provider. In certain customer TOB transactions,  the 
Firm, as liquidity provider, has entered into a 
reimbursement agreement with the Residual holder.

protect Residual holders from potential losses on any of the 
underlying municipal bonds.  The Firm does not consolidate 
customer TOB trusts, since  the Firm does not have the 
power to make decisions that significantly impact the 
economic performance of the municipal bond vehicle.  The Firm’s maximum exposure as a liquidity provider to

Maximum liquidity exposure was $6.9B at June 30, 2022 ($6.8B at Dec 31, 2021); fair value of VIE assets was $9.4B and $10.5B, respectively.
- Loan securitizations: The Firm securitizes and sells residential mortgages (prime), credit card receivables, and commercial mortgages. For nonconsolidated Firm‑sponsored entities where sale accounting was achieved, the disclosure provides quarterly and year‑to‑date activity (principal securitized; proceeds received as financial instruments, largely Level 2; servicing fees; interest cash flows). Re‑securitizations are excluded; loans at fair value had carrying values approximating sale proceeds; “commercial and other” includes commercial mortgage and other consumer loans; activity excludes GSE/government agency securitizations.

The Firm does not consolidate these vehicles and shares a portion of credit risk on a limited number of sales. Activity for the periods shows significant loan sales with proceeds largely received as Level 2 securities that are generally sold shortly after or retained in investment securities; gains/losses on sales were minimal.
- Options to repurchase delinquent loans: Beyond repurchases for representation and warranty breaches, the Firm may and typically does repurchase delinquent loans it services for Ginnie Mae and certain other agencies to continue servicing or manage foreclosure; such loans remain insured/guaranteed. When the option is exercisable, the loans and a corresponding liability are recognized on balance sheet. As of June 30, 2022: $826M of loans repurchased or subject to option (predominantly from Ginnie Mae pools), $8M of real estate owned, and $25M of foreclosed government‑guaranteed residential mortgage loans (vs. $1,022M, $5M, and $36M at Dec 31, 2021).
- Delinquencies and liquidation losses in private‑label securitizations: For nonconsolidated Firm‑sponsored private‑label securitizations with continuing involvement, the Firm discloses outstanding balances, 90+ day delinquencies, and net liquidation losses/recoveries by asset type. As of June 30, 2022: total securitized loans $172.2B (up from $150.8B at Dec 31, 2021), with $4.1B 90+ days past due (down from $5.5B). Net liquidation results showed modest recoveries in 2022 versus losses in 2021.

Goodwill impairment testing
Goodwill is tested for impairment during the fourth quarter 
of each fiscal year, or more often if events or 
circumstances, such as adverse changes in the business 
climate, indicate that there may be an impairment.  Refer to 
Note  15 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 10-K for a further 
discussion of  the Firm’s goodwill impairment testing.
Unanticipated declines in business performance, increases 
in credit losses, increases in capital requirements, as well as 
deterioration in economic or market conditions, adverse 
regulatory or legislative changes or increases in the 
estimated market cost of equity, could cause the estimated 
fair values of the  Firm’s reporting units to decline in the 
future, which could result in a material impairment charge 
to earnings in a future period related to some portion of the 
associated goodwill.  
As of  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, the Firm reviewed current economic 
conditions, estimated market cost of equity, as well as 
actual business results and projections of business 
performance . Based on such reviews, the Firm has

2022 , or D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, nor was goodwill written off

title: Mortgage servicing rights
heading: Mortgage servicing right s
start_phrase: MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others.
summary:
- Defines mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) as the fair value of expected future cash flows from servicing loans for others, valued by estimated servicing fees and ancillary income minus servicing costs; MSRs amortize over time as cash flows are realized and are recognized when purchased or when loans are sold/securitized with servicing retained.
- Summarizes MSR activity for Q2 and first half of 2022 vs 2021, including:
  - Beginning and ending fair values (ending June 30, 2022: $7.4B vs $4.5B in 2021).
  - Originations, purchases, and dispositions (including transfers of excess MSRs to agency trusts in exchange for SMBS).
  - Changes due to collection/realization of expected cash flows.
  - Valuation changes driven by market interest rates/prepayment dynamics and by other model inputs (projected cash flows, discount rates, and non-rate prepayment changes).
  - Unrealized gains/losses recognized in income.
- Provides servicing portfolio metrics:
  - Third-party mortgage loans serviced outstanding ($576B at June 30, 2022 vs $465B in 2021).
  - Servicer advances outstanding ($1.2B vs $1.7B) with minimal credit risk due to reimbursement priority and contractual protections.
- Details mortgage fees and related income for Consumer & Community Banking (CCB):
  - Production revenue significantly lower in 2022 vs 2021.
  - Net mortgage servicing revenue broken into operating revenue (loan servicing revenue and the negative impact from realization of expected MSR cash flows) and risk management (MSR fair value changes from rates/other inputs and offsetting derivative results).
  - Overall, higher servicing-related revenue in 2022 offset by weaker production and hedge impacts; totals presented for three and six months.
- Clarifies that “market interest rates and other” captures both estimated and actual prepayment effects; “other inputs” include cost to service, discount rates, and non-rate prepayment factors (e.g., home prices).
- Presents key MSR valuation assumptions and sensitivities:
  - Weighted-average constant prepayment rate (CPR) and option-adjusted spread (OAS) at June 30, 2022 vs December 31, 2021.
  - Hypothetical adverse-change sensitivities showing MSR fair value declines under higher CPRs and wider OAS (including operational/regulatory capital effects).
- Overall themes: rising rates in 2022 increased MSR fair values and servicing revenues while originations/production revenue declined; servicing portfolio grew and servicer advances decreased year over year.
text:
MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others. The fair value 
considers estimated future servicing fees and ancillary revenue, offset by estimated costs to service the loans, and generally 
declines over time as net servicing cash flows are received, effectively amortizing the MSR asset against contractual servicing 
and ancillary fee income. MSRs are either purchased from third parties or recognized upon sale or securitization of mortgage 
loans if servicing is retained. Refer to Note s 2 and 15 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021  Form 10-K  for a further description of the 
MSR asset, interest rate risk management, and the valuation of MSRs.

title: Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
heading: Note 19 – Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
start_phrase: AOCI includes the after-tax change in unrealized gains and losses on investment securities, foreign currency translation adjustments (including the impact of related derivatives), fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges, cash flow hedging activities, net loss and prior service costs/(credit) related to the Firm’s defined benefit pension and OPEB plans, and fair value option-elected liabilities arising from changes in the Firm’s own credit risk (DVA).
summary:
- Scope and definition: Note 19 explains what comprises Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI): after-tax unrealized gains/losses on investment securities; foreign currency translation adjustments (including related hedges); fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges; cash flow hedging activities; net loss and prior service cost/(credit) for defined benefit pension and OPEB plans; and changes in the Firm’s own credit risk on fair value option–elected liabilities (DVA).

- Periods covered: Detailed reconciliations for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, showing beginning balances, net changes by component, and ending AOCI balances.

- AOCI balances:
  - June 30, 2022: total AOCI of $(14,369) million (down from $(9,567) million at April 1, 2022 and from $(84) million at January 1, 2022).
  - June 30, 2021: total AOCI of $2,570 million (up from $1,041 million at April 1, 2021; down from $7,986 million at January 1, 2021).

- Key drivers of Q2 2022 after-tax OCI movement (net change of $(4,802) million):
  - Significant losses: unrealized losses on investment securities $(4,031) million; cash flow hedges $(1,348) million; translation adjustments $(679) million.
  - Offsets: DVA +$1,185 million; fair value hedges (excluded components) +$51 million; pension/OPEB +$20 million.

- Key drivers of 1H 2022 after-tax OCI movement (net change of $(14,285) million):
  - Significant losses: unrealized losses on investment securities $(11,484) million; cash flow hedges $(4,139) million; translation adjustments $(741) million.
  - Offsets: DVA +$1,831 million; fair value hedges (excluded components) +$161 million; pension/OPEB +$87 million.

- Comparative 2021 movements:
  - Q2 2021 after-tax OCI gain of $1,529 million driven by gains on investment securities and cash flow hedges, partially offset by translation and fair value hedge losses; DVA contributed positively.
  - 1H 2021 after-tax OCI loss of $(5,416) million, primarily from unrealized losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges, partly offset by translation hedge gains and DVA.

- Translation adjustments and hedges: The note discloses separate lines for translation effects and related hedges, showing offsets (e.g., Q2 2022 translation after-tax $(3,357) million versus hedge after-tax +$2,678 million).

- Reclassification adjustments and presentation:
  - Realized gains/losses on investment securities reclassified to Investment securities gains/(losses).
  - Translation and related hedge reclassifications recorded in other income/expense (amounts not material for the periods shown).
  - Fair value hedges line reflects changes in cross-currency basis spreads excluded from effectiveness; initial costs recognized in interest accruals.
  - Cash flow hedge reclassifications primarily recorded in noninterest revenue, net interest income, and compensation expense.

- AFS-to-HTM transfers: As of June 30, 2022 and 2021, AOCI includes after-tax net unamortized unrealized gains/(losses) related to AFS securities transferred to HTM of $(1.4) billion and $3.0 billion, respectively.

- Overall takeaway: In 2022, AOCI declined sharply into a larger accumulated loss, driven mainly by sizable unrealized losses on investment securities and adverse cash flow hedge marks, partially offset by positive DVA; 2021 showed mixed results with Q2 positive OCI but a year-to-date decline versus beginning of year.

title: Restricted cash and other restricted assets
heading: Note 20 – Restricted cash and other restricted assets
start_phrase: Refer to Note 26 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion of the Firm’s restricted cash and other restricted assets.
summary:
- Note 20 – Restricted cash and other restricted assets:
  - Explains that portions of the Firm’s cash and other assets are restricted by U.S. and non-U.S. regulatory authorities, including broker-dealer rules, based on activities of subsidiaries.
  - Details restricted cash components and balances:
    - Segregated for the benefit of securities and cleared derivative customers: $19.8B at June 30, 2022 vs. $14.6B at December 31, 2021.
    - Cash reserves at non-U.S. central banks and held for other general purposes: $7.6B vs. $5.1B.
    - Total restricted cash: $27.4B vs. $19.7B, comprising $26.1B/$18.4B in deposits with banks and $1.3B/$1.3B in cash and due from banks.
  - Other restricted assets:
    - Cash and securities pledged with clearing organizations for the benefit of customers: $42.8B vs. $47.5B.
    - Securities restricted in relation to customer activity (fair value): $43.2B vs. $30.0B.

- Note 21 – Regulatory capital:
  - Summarizes U.S. regulatory capital frameworks applicable to the consolidated holding company (Federal Reserve) and the principal insured depository institution (OCC), covering risk-based (CET1, Tier 1, Total) and leverage-based (Tier 1 leverage, SLR) requirements and well-capitalized thresholds.
  - Highlights that holding company requirements incorporate a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2) and, for Standardized ratios, a 3.2% stress capital buffer; Advanced approaches include a 2.5% capital conservation buffer. IDI subsidiaries are not subject to the GSIB surcharge but include a 2.5% buffer.
  - Notes leverage requirements, including minimum SLR (3%) plus supplementary buffers of 2.0% for the holding company and 3.0% for IDIs; well-capitalized thresholds are defined for IDIs (e.g., Tier 1 leverage 5% and SLR 6%) but not for holding companies.
  - Describes CECL regulatory capital transition: the two-year deferral ended December 31, 2021; beginning January 1, 2022, the $2.9B benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years. As of June 30, 2022, CET1 includes a remaining $2.2B benefit; 25% of other CECL transition effects were also phased out from Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.

title: Regulatory capital - Introduction
heading: Note 21 – Regulatory capital
start_phrase: Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory capital requirements as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021: the Federal Reserve sets consolidated bank holding company (BHC) standards and the OCC/FDIC set minimums and well-capitalized thresholds for the Firm’s insured depository institution (IDI) subsidiaries (JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.); the Firm must maintain CET1, Tier 1, Total risk-based capital, Tier 1 leverage, and SLR minimums or face potential Federal Reserve action. Risk-based requirements shown are BHC Standardized CET1/Tier 1/Total of 11.2%/12.7%/14.7 and BHC Advanced 10.5%/12.0%/14.0; IDI Standardized/Advanced 7.0%/8.5%/10.5. Well-capitalized thresholds are (BHC/IDI): CET1 NA/6.5%, Tier 1 6.0%/8.0%, Total 10.0%/10.0%. Leverage-based minimums are Tier 1 leverage 4.0% (BHC/IDI) and SLR 5.0%/6.0% (BHC/IDI), with IDI well-capitalized at 5.0% (Tier 1 leverage) and 6.0% (SLR); no BHC well-capitalized leverage thresholds. Requirements incorporate buffers: BHC ratios include a 3.5% GSIB Method 2 surcharge plus a 3.2% stress capital buffer for Basel III Standardized and a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Basel III Advanced; IDIs include a 2.5% conservation buffer; the countercyclical buffer is 0%. Refer to 2021 Form 10-K Note 27 for further detail.

a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
