title: CECL regulatory capital transition
heading: CECL regulatory capital transition
start_phrase: On December 31, 2021, the CECL capital transition provisions ,	which delayed the effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, expired.
summary:
- Scope and regulators: Outlines U.S. regulatory capital requirements applicable to JPMorgan Chase & Co. (as a bank holding company, BHC, supervised by the Federal Reserve) and its principal insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (supervised by the OCC), with FDIC involvement for IDI standards. References Note 27 of the 2021 Form 10‑K for additional detail.

- Required capital measures: Describes minimum and “well-capitalized” thresholds the Firm and its IDI must meet for:
  - Risk-based ratios: CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital, and Total capital.
  - Leverage-based ratios: Tier 1 leverage ratio and Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
  - Notes that failing to meet minimums could prompt regulatory action.

- Risk-based ratio thresholds (as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Presents tables of required ratios under both Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for the BHC and IDI, plus well-capitalized thresholds.
  - BHC requirements include: minimums plus a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2), a 3.2% Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) for Standardized ratios, and a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced ratios; the countercyclical buffer is 0%.
  - IDI requirements include a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer; IDIs are not subject to the GSIB surcharge.
  - Notes well-capitalized thresholds for BHCs (risk-based) and IDIs per applicable regulations.

- Leverage-based thresholds:
  - Provides minimum Tier 1 leverage and SLR requirements for BHC and IDI, including composition of the SLR (3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% for BHCs and 3.0% for IDIs).
  - Lists well-capitalized leverage thresholds for IDIs; Fed regulations do not set well-capitalized thresholds for BHC leverage measures.

- CECL regulatory capital transition:
  - The two-year delay of CECL’s impact on regulatory capital expired December 31, 2021.
  - Starting January 1, 2022, the $2.9 billion CET1 benefit recognized at year-end 2021 is being phased out 25% per year over three years; $2.2 billion remained in CET1 at June 30, 2022.
  - Also phases out 25% of other CECL transition amounts from Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
  - References Note 27 of the 2021 Form 10‑K for more on CECL transition.

- Reported capital metrics:
  - Provides detailed tables (for June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021) of CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital; risk-weighted assets; and resulting capital ratios under both Basel III Standardized and Advanced for the Firm and the Bank.
  - Presents leverage metrics: adjusted average assets, Tier 1 leverage ratio, total leverage exposure, and SLR.
  - Notes that metrics reflect CECL transition provisions and that PPP loans receive a 0% risk weight.

- Capital status: Confirms that as of both dates, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. were well-capitalized and met all applicable capital requirements.

CECL regulatory capital transition
On December 31, 2021, the CECL capital transition 
provisions ,	which delayed the effects of CECL on regulatory 
capital for two years, expired. Beginning January 1, 2022, 
the $ 2 . 9  b i l l i o n CECL capital benefit recognized as of

over a three-year period.  As of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, CET1 capital 
reflected the remaining $ 2 . 2  b i l l i o n, benefit associated with 
the CECL capital transition provisions.
Additionally, effective January 1, 2022, the Firm phased 
out 25% of the other relevant CECL capital transition 
provisions recognized as of December 31, 2021, from Tier 
2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage 
exposure.  
Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021  Form 10-K for 
further information on CECL capital transition provisions.

summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s off‑balance sheet lending‑related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments, explaining that contractual amounts represent maximum possible credit risk but often are not drawn and thus overstate expected exposure; the Firm maintains an allowance for credit losses on such commitments (see Note 12) and refers to accounting policies in 2021 Form 10‑K Note 28. A table summarizes contractual amounts and carrying values by remaining maturity at June 30, 2022 and Dec 31, 2021: total lending‑related contractual amount $1.302T ($1.262T prior) with carrying value $2.868B ($2.624B); consumer total $814.5B including $774.0B credit card lines (the Firm can reduce/cancel certain lines, typically closes cards 60+ days past due, and may reduce/close HELOCs for collateral or creditworthiness declines); wholesale total $487.5B including $455.4B other unfunded commitments, $28.1B standby letters/financial guarantees, and $4.0B other letters (carrying value $2.743B). Other guarantees/commitments include securities lending indemnification agreements $337.0B (collateral held $355.2B), derivatives qualifying as guarantees $54.2B, unsettled resale/borrowed $195.3B, unsettled repo/loaned $99.4B, exchange and clearing house guarantees $127.7B, loans sold with recourse $0.8B, and other $11.3B; certain amounts are shown net of risk participations, and carrying values reflect allowances/guarantee liabilities or fair value, including markdowns on held‑for‑sale unfunded bridge commitments at June 30, 2022.
text:
Off–balance sheet lending-related 
financial instruments, guarantees, and other 
commitments
JPMorgan Chase  provides lending-related financial 
instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) to address 
the financing needs of its customers and clients. The 
contractual amount of these financial instruments 
represents the maximum possible credit risk to  the Firm 
should the customer or client draw upon the commitment 
or the Firm  be required to fulfill its obligation under the 
guarantee, and should the customer or client subsequently 
fail to perform according to the terms of the contract. Most 
of these commitments and guarantees have historically 
been refinanced, extended, cancelled, or expired without 
being drawn or a default occurring. As a result, the total 
contractual amount of these instruments is not, in  the 
Firm’s view, representative of its expected future credit 
exposure or funding requirements.  Refer to Note  28 of 
JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021  Form 10-K  for a further discussion 
of lending-related commitments and guarantees, and the  
Firm’s related accounting policies.  
To provide for expected  credit losses in wholesale and 
certain consumer lending-related commitments, an 
allowance for credit losses on lending-related commitments 
is maintained. Refer to Note  12 for further information 
regarding the allowance for credit losses on lending-related 
commitments .The following table summarizes the contractual amounts 
and carrying values of off-balance sheet lending-related 
financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments 
at J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1. The amounts in 
the table below for credit card, home equity and certain 
scored business banking lending-related commitments 
represent the total available credit for these products.  The 
Firm has not experienced, and does not anticipate, that all 
available lines of credit for these products will be utilized at 
the same time.  The Firm can reduce or cancel credit card 
and certain scored business banking lines of credit by 
providing the borrower notice or, in some cases as 
permitted by law, without notice. In addition,  the Firm 
typically closes credit card lines when the borrower is  60 
days  or more past due.  The Firm may reduce or close 
HELOCs when there are significant decreases in the value of 
the underlying property, or when there has been a 
demonstrable decline in the creditworthiness of the 
borrower.

heading: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
start_phrase: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit generally consist of commitments for working capital and general corporate purposes, extensions of credit to support commercial paper facilities and bond financings in the event that those obligations cannot be remarketed to new investors,
summary:
- Scope: Disclosure of off-balance-sheet and contingent obligations, including unfunded commitments to extend credit, standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, certain derivatives that qualify as guarantees, and merchant charge-back exposures.

- Unfunded commitments to extend credit: Primarily for working capital and general corporate purposes; backstops for commercial paper and bond financings if not remarketed; committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations; multipurpose facilities that may be drawn in various forms, including standby letters of credit.

- Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees: Conditional commitments guaranteeing a client’s performance to third parties for transactions such as commercial paper, bond and acquisition financings, and trade finance.

- Credit quality and amounts (internal risk ratings basis):
  - As of June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021
    - Total contractual amounts:
      - Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees: $28.051B (vs. $28.530B)
      - Other letters of credit: $4.006B (vs. $4.448B)
    - Investment-grade: $19.696B (vs. $19.998B) for standby/other guarantees; $2.763B (vs. $3.087B) for other LCs
    - Noninvestment-grade: $8.355B (vs. $8.532B) for standby/other guarantees; $1.243B (vs. $1.361B) for other LCs
    - Allowance for lending-related commitments: $97M (vs. $123M) for standby/other guarantees; $19M (vs. $9M) for other LCs
    - Guarantee liability: $320M (vs. $353M)
    - Total carrying value: $417M (vs. $476M) for standby/other guarantees; $19M (vs. $9M) for other LCs
    - Commitments with collateral: $15.314B (vs. $14.511B) for standby/other guarantees; $690M (vs. $999M) for other LCs

- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees (U.S. GAAP):
  - Notional amounts: Derivative guarantees $54.183B (vs. $55.730B)
  - Stable value contracts: Notional $28.480B (vs. $29.778B); maximum exposure $2.635B (vs. $2.882B)
  - Fair value derivative payables: $842M (vs. $475M)
  - The firm also both purchases and sells credit protection via credit derivatives.

- Merchant charge-backs: As a merchant acquirer, the firm has contingent liability for disputed card transactions; if unrecoverable from merchants, the firm bears the loss. Risk mitigants include withholding future settlements, holding reserve accounts, obtaining collateral, and recognizing a valuation allowance for payment/performance risk.
text:
Other unfunded commitments to extend credit generally 
consist of commitments for working capital and general 
corporate purposes, extensions of credit to support 
commercial paper facilities and bond financings in the event 
that those obligations cannot be remarketed to new 
investors, as well as committed liquidity facilities to clearing 
organizations.  The Firm also issues commitments under 
multipurpose facilities which could be drawn upon in 
several forms, including the issuance of a standby letter of 
credit.

title: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
heading: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
start_phrase: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees are conditional lending commitments issued by the Firm to guarantee the performance of a client or customer to a third party under certain arrangements,
summary:
- Focus: The Firm’s off-balance sheet exposures related to unfunded commitments, standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, derivatives that qualify as guarantees, and merchant charge-back contingencies, with balances as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Other unfunded commitments to extend credit: Include commitments for working capital and general corporate purposes, backstops for commercial paper facilities and bond financings when remarketing fails, committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations, and multipurpose facilities that can be drawn in various forms (including standby letters of credit).
- Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees: Conditional lending commitments that guarantee a client’s performance to third parties in transactions such as CP facilities, bond and acquisition financings, and trade financings.
  - Contractual amounts at June 30, 2022: $28.051B for standby letters/other financial guarantees (IG $19.696B; non-IG $8.355B) and $4.006B for other letters of credit (IG $2.763B; non-IG $1.243B). At Dec 31, 2021: $28.530B and $4.448B, respectively.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments: $97M (standby/guarantees) and $19M (other LCs) at June 30, 2022; $123M and $9M at Dec 31, 2021.
  - Guarantee liability: $320M at June 30, 2022; $353M at Dec 31, 2021.
  - Total carrying value: $417M (standby/guarantees) and $19M (other LCs) at June 30, 2022; $476M and $9M at Dec 31, 2021.
  - Commitments with collateral: $15.314B (standby/guarantees) and $690M (other LCs) at June 30, 2022; $14.511B and $999M at Dec 31, 2021.
  - Credit quality referenced to the Firm’s internal risk ratings.
- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees (under U.S. GAAP):
  - Notional amounts at June 30, 2022: $54.183B (derivative guarantees) and $28.480B (stable value contracts with contractually limited exposure); $55.730B and $29.778B at Dec 31, 2021.
  - Maximum exposure of stable value contracts: $2.635B at June 30, 2022; $2.882B at Dec 31, 2021.
  - Fair value of derivative payables: $842M at June 30, 2022; $475M at Dec 31, 2021.
  - The Firm also both purchases and sells credit protection via credit derivatives.
- Merchant charge-backs: As a merchant acquirer, the Firm retains contingent liability for disputed card transactions. If a dispute favors the cardholder and recovery from the merchant fails, the Firm bears the loss. Risk is mitigated through withheld settlements, cash reserves, collateral, and a valuation allowance for expected charge-back losses.
- Cross-references: Notes on internal risk ratings and additional details on derivatives and credit derivatives are referenced to other disclosures.

title: Merchant charge-backs
heading: Merchant charge-backs
start_phrase: Under the rules of payment networks, the Firm, in its role as a merchant acquirer, retains a contingent liability for disputed processed credit and debit card transactions that result in a charge-back to the merchant.
summary:
- Scope: Discloses JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance sheet exposures related to unfunded credit commitments, standby letters of credit, financial guarantees, certain derivatives that qualify as guarantees, and merchant charge-back contingencies.

- Other unfunded commitments to extend credit: Primarily commitments for working capital and general corporate purposes, backstops for commercial paper and bond financings when remarketing fails, and committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations; includes multipurpose facilities that can be drawn in various forms, such as standby letters of credit.

- Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees: Conditional lending commitments that guarantee a client’s performance to third parties in arrangements like commercial paper and bond financings, acquisition and trade financings, and similar transactions.

- Quantitative summary (June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021):
  - Total contractual amounts: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees $28.1B (vs. $28.5B); Other letters of credit $4.0B (vs. $4.4B).
  - Credit quality categories: Presented by investment-grade and noninvestment-grade based on the Firm’s internal risk ratings.
  - Allowance and guarantee liability: Allowance for lending-related commitments $97M and $19M (vs. $123M and $9M); Guarantee liability $320M (vs. $353M).
  - Total carrying value: $417M for standby/other guarantees and $19M for other letters of credit (vs. $476M and $9M).
  - Commitments with collateral: $15.3B for standby/other guarantees and $0.7B for other letters of credit (vs. $14.5B and $1.0B).

  - Stable value contracts: Notional $28.5B (vs. $29.8B) with maximum exposure capped at $2.6B (vs. $2.9B).
  - Fair value of related derivative payables: $842M (vs. $475M).
  - The Firm also participates as both buyer and seller of credit protection via credit derivatives.

- Merchant charge-backs: As a merchant acquirer, the Firm holds contingent liability for disputed card transactions; if unable to recover from merchants after charge-backs, it bears the loss. Risk is mitigated through withheld settlements, cash reserves, collateral, and a valuation allowance for payment/performance risk.
text:
Merchant charge-backs  
Under the rules of payment networks,  the Firm, in its role as 
a merchant acquirer, retains a contingent liability for 
disputed processed credit and debit card transactions that 
result in a charge-back to the merchant. If a dispute is 
resolved in the cardholder’s favor, Merchant Services will 
(through the cardholder’s issuing bank) credit or refund the 
amount to the cardholder and will charge back the 
transaction to the merchant. If Merchant Services is unable 
to collect the amount from the merchant, Merchant Services 
will bear the loss for the amount credited or refunded to the 
cardholder. Merchant Services mitigates this risk by 
withholding future settlements, retaining cash reserve 
accounts or obtaining other collateral. In addition, Merchant 
Services recognizes a valuation allowance that covers the 
payment or performance risk to  the Firm related to charge-
backs.

title: Contingencies
heading: Contingencies
start_phrase: As of June 30, 2022, the Firm and its subsidiaries and affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government investigations or regulatory enforcement matters.
summary:
- The note discloses broad litigation contingencies across the Firm’s lines of business and geographies, encompassing private civil litigations (from single-plaintiff to class actions), government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters, including tort, contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection claims, some involving novel legal theories.
- As of June 30, 2022, the Firm estimates the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves to be $0 to approximately $1.2 billion. The estimate excludes matters where a loss range cannot be estimated and reflects significant judgment due to early case stages, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification), and uncertain outcomes; actual losses may differ materially and the estimate will change over time.
- Material proceedings summarized:
  - Amrapali (India): The Enforcement Directorate is investigating J.P. Morgan India Private Limited regarding 2010 and 2012 investments by offshore funds in Amrapali Group housing projects. Homebuyers’ petitions are being overseen by India’s Supreme Court. In August 2021, the ED fined J.P. Morgan India about $31.5 million; the Firm is appealing. In July 2019, the Supreme Court made preliminary findings referencing possible violations of currency control and money laundering provisions by Amrapali and other parties, including unspecified JPMorgan entities and the offshore funds, and directed further ED inquiry under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, the ED attached about $25 million from J.P. Morgan India; the Firm is cooperating.
  - Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account holding approximately $1.1 billion for Nigeria’s federal government and two oil companies related to an oil field dispute. Following client-directed payouts in 2011 and 2013, Nigeria sued in the English High Court in November 2017 seeking approximately $875 million, alleging the Bank should have been on notice of a client fraud. After a February–April 2022 trial, the Court dismissed the claim in June 2022 in JPMorgan’s favor. Nigeria has sought permission to appeal limited to the 2013 payment of approximately $75 million.
  - Foreign exchange matters: The Firm references earlier settlements with authorities concerning FX sales and trading activities and related controls, noting that in May 2015 the Firm pleaded (details truncated in the excerpt).

Contingencies 
As of June 30, 2022, the Firm and its subsidiaries and 
affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal 
proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government 
investigations or regulatory enforcement matters. The 
litigations range from individual actions involving a single 
plaintiff to class action lawsuits with potentially millions of 
class members. Investigations and regulatory enforcement 
matters involve both formal and informal proceedings, by 
both governmental agencies and self-regulatory 
organizations. These legal proceedings are at varying stages 
of adjudication, arbitration or investigation, and involve 
each of the Firm’s lines of business and several geographies 
and a wide variety of claims (including common law tort 
and contract claims and statutory antitrust, securities and 
consumer protection claims), some of which present novel 
legal theories.
The Firm believes the estimate of the aggregate range of 
reasonably possible losses, in excess of reserves 
established, for its legal proceedings is from $0 to 
approximately $1.2 billion  at June 30, 2022. This estimated 
aggregate range of reasonably possible losses was based 
upon information available as of that date for those 
proceedings in which the Firm believes that an estimate of 
reasonably possible loss can be made. For certain matters, 
the Firm does not believe that such an estimate can be 
made, as of that date. The Firm’s estimate of the aggregate 
range of reasonably possible losses involves significant 
judgment, given:
•the number, variety and varying stages of the 
proceedings, including the fact that many are in 
preliminary stages, 
•the existence in many such proceedings of multiple 
defendants, including the Firm, whose share of liability 
(if any) has yet to be determined, 
•the numerous yet-unresolved issues in many of the 
proceedings, including issues regarding class 
certification and the scope of many of the claims, and 
•the attendant uncertainty of the various potential 
outcomes of such proceedings, including where the Firm 
has made assumptions concerning future rulings by the 
court or other adjudicator, or about the behavior or 
incentives of adverse parties or regulatory authorities, 
and those assumptions prove to be incorrect.
In addition, the outcome of a particular proceeding may be 
a result which the Firm did not take into account in its 
estimate because the Firm had deemed the likelihood of 
that outcome to be remote. Accordingly, the Firm’s 
estimate of the aggregate range of reasonably possible 
losses will change from time to time, and actual losses may 
vary significantly.Set forth below are descriptions of the Firm’s material legal 
proceedings.

Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation.  JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A. operated an escrow and depository account for the 
Federal Government of Nigeria (“FGN”) and two major 
international oil companies. The account held 
approximately $1.1 billion  in connection with a dispute 
among the clients over rights to an oil field. Following the 
settlement of the dispute, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. paid 
out the monies in the account in 2011 and 2013 in 
accordance with directions received from its clients. In 
November 2017, the Federal Republic of Nigeria (“FRN”) 
commenced a claim in the English High Court for 
approximately $875 million  in payments made out of the 
accounts. The FRN alleged that the payments were 
instructed as part of a complex fraud not involving 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., but that JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A. was or should have been on notice that the payments 
may be fraudulent. A trial was held between February and 
April 2022. In June 2022, the Court decided the case in 
favor of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and dismissed it in full. 
The FRN has requested permission to appeal the decision 
relating solely to the 2013 payment of approximately 
$ 7 5  m i l l i o n.

title: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation.
heading: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation.
start_phrase: The Firm previously reported settlements with certain government authorities relating to its foreign exchange (“FX”) sales and trading activities and controls related to those activities.
summary:

This estimate involves significant judgment due to the number and stages of matters, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope), and uncertain outcomes; the range may change, and actual losses could vary significantly.

- Amrapali (India): ED investigation into 2010 and 2012 investments by offshore funds formerly managed by JPMorgan entities in Amrapali Group housing projects. In 2021, ED fined J.P. Morgan India Private Limited approximately $31.5 million (under appeal). The Supreme Court of India made preliminary findings in 2019 regarding potential currency control and money laundering violations and ordered further inquiry under PMLA and FEMA. In 2020, ED attached approximately $25 million from J.P. Morgan India Private Limited. The Firm is cooperating.

FRN sued in 2017 for approximately $875 million alleging the Bank should have suspected fraud. After a 2022 trial, the Court ruled for JPMorgan and dismissed the case in full; FRN seeks permission to appeal as to the 2013 ~$75 million payment only.

- Foreign exchange (FX) investigations and litigation:
  - Governmental: Prior settlements include a 2015 guilty plea to a federal antitrust violation; the Department of Labor granted a five-year QPAM exemption under ERISA through January 2023, with a further exemption needed thereafter. The only remaining governmental inquiry is before the South Africa Competition Tribunal.

  - Monetary class: A 2018 amended settlement added $900 million to ~ $5.3 billion from the original settlement; approved in 2019, with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants.

Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation.  The Firm 
previously reported settlements with certain government 
authorities relating to its foreign exchange (“FX”) sales and 
trading activities and controls related to those activities. 
Among those resolutions, in May 2015, the Firm pleaded 
173guilty to a single violation of federal antitrust law. The 
Department of Labor granted the Firm a five-year  
exemption of disqualification that allows the Firm and its 
affiliates to continue to rely on the Qualified Professional 
Asset Manager exemption under the Employee Retirement 
Income Security Act (“ERISA”) until January 2023. The Firm 
will need the Department of Labor to approve a further 
exemption to cover the remainder of the ten-year  
disqualification period following the antitrust plea. The only 
remaining FX-related governmental inquiry is a South Africa 
Competition Commission matter which is currently pending 
before the South Africa Competition Tribunal.
With respect to civil litigation matters, in August 2018, the 
United States District Court for the Southern District of New 
York granted final approval to the Firm’s settlement of a 
consolidated class action brought by U.S.-based plaintiffs, 
which principally alleged violations of federal antitrust laws 
based on an alleged conspiracy to manipulate foreign 
exchange rates and also sought damages on behalf of 
persons who transacted in FX futures and options on 
futures. Certain members of the settlement class filed 
requests to the Court to be excluded from the class, and 
certain of them filed a complaint against the Firm and other 
foreign exchange dealers in November 2018. A number of 
these actions remain pending. Further, a putative class 
action has been filed against the Firm and other foreign 
exchange dealers on behalf of certain consumers who 
purchased foreign currencies at allegedly inflated rates. 
Another putative class action was brought against the Firm 
and other foreign exchange dealers on behalf of purported 
indirect purchasers of FX instruments. In 2020, the Court 
approved a settlement by the Firm and 11 other defendants 
of that class action for a total of $10 million . In addition, 
some FX-related individual and putative class actions based 
on similar alleged underlying conduct have been filed 
outside the U.S., including in the U.K., Israel, the 
Netherlands, Brazil and Australia. In a putative class action 
pending before the U.K. Competition Appeal Tribunal, the 
tribunal has denied a request by the proposed class 
representatives for class certification on an opt-out basis.

text:
Inquiries Concerning Preservation Requirements . In 
December 2021 certain of the Firm’s subsidiaries entered 
into resolutions with the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (“SEC”) and the U.S. Commodity Futures 
Trading Commission (“CFTC”) to resolve their respective 
civil investigations of compliance with records preservation 
requirements applicable to broker-dealer firms, swap 
dealers and futures commission merchants. The SEC and 
CFTC found that J.P. Morgan Securities LLC did not maintain 
copies of certain communications required to be maintained 
under their respective record keeping rules, where such 
communications were sent or received by employees over 
electronic messaging channels that had not been approved 
for employee use by the Firm. The CFTC resolution also 
included JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and J.P. Morgan 
Securities plc as swap dealers. The SEC and CFTC also found 
related supervision failures. Under these resolutions, J.P. Morgan Securities LLC paid a $ 1 2 5  m i l l i o n civil monetary 
penalty to the SEC, and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and J.P. Morgan Securities plc 
paid a total $ 7 5  m i l l i o n civil monetary penalty to the CFTC. 
The Firm continues to respond to requests for information 
and other material from certain authorities concerning its 
compliance with records preservation requirements in 
connection with business communications sent over 
electronic messaging channels that have not been approved 
by the Firm. The Firm is cooperating with these inquiries.
In March 2022, a shareholder derivative action was filed in 
the United States District Court for the Eastern District of 
New York against the Firm’s Board of Directors asserting 
breaches of fiduciary duty and violation of federal securities 
laws based on the Board’s alleged failure to exercise 
adequate oversight over compliance with records 
preservation requirements. The complaint seeks damages, 
restitution, disgorgement and corporate governance 
reforms. Defendants have moved to dismiss the complaint.

title: Interchange Litigation.
heading: Interchange Litigation.
start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
summary:
- Criminal antitrust matter (FX): The Firm pled guilty to a federal antitrust violation, triggering a 10-year ERISA QPAM disqualification. Penalties totaled $200 million ($125 million to the SEC; $75 million to the CFTC), involving J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities plc. text:
Interchange Litigation. Groups of merchants and retail 
associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging 
that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, 
conspired to set the price of credit and debit card 
interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of 
antitrust laws. In 2012, the parties initially settled the cases 
for a cash payment, a temporary reduction of credit card 
interchange, and modifications to certain credit card 
network rules. In 2017, after the approval of that 
settlement was reversed on appeal, the case was remanded 
to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of 
New York for further proceedings consistent with the 
appellate decision.
The original class action was divided into two separate 
actions, one seeking primarily monetary relief and the other 
seeking primarily injunctive relief. In September 2018, the 
parties to the monetary class action finalized an agreement 
which amends and supersedes the prior settlement 
agreement. Pursuant to this settlement, the defendants 
collectively contributed an additional $900 million  to the 
approximately $5.3 billion  previously held in escrow from 
the original settlement. In December 2019, the amended 
settlement agreement was approved by the District Court. 
Certain merchants appealed the District Court’s approval 
order, and those appeals are pending. Based on the 
percentage of merchants that opted out of the amended 
class settlement, $700 million  has been returned to the 
defendants from the settlement escrow in accordance with 
the settlement agreement. The injunctive class action 
continues separately, and in September 2021, the District 
Court granted plaintiffs’ motion for class certification in 
part, and denied the motion in part.
In addition, certain merchants have filed individual actions 
raising similar allegations against Visa and Mastercard, as 
well as against the Firm and other banks, and some of those 
actions remain pending.

heading: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation.

- JPMorgan Chase is addressing global regulatory inquiries into benchmark rates, focusing on BBA-administered LIBOR (multiple currencies) and EBF’s EURIBOR.

text:
LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and 
Litigation.  JPMorgan Chase has responded to inquiries from 
various governmental agencies and entities around the 
world relating primarily to the British Bankers Association’s 
(“BBA”) London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) for 
various currencies and the European Banking Federation’s 
Euro Interbank Offered Rate (“EURIBOR”). The Swiss 
Competition Commission’s investigation relating to 
EURIBOR, to which the Firm and one other bank remain 
subject, continues. In December 2016, the European 
Commission issued a decision against the Firm and other 
banks finding an infringement of European antitrust rules 
relating to EURIBOR. The Firm has filed an appeal of that 
decision with the European General Court, and that appeal 
is pending.
In addition, the Firm has been named as a defendant along 
with other banks in various individual and putative class 
actions related to benchmark rates, including U.S. dollar 
LIBOR. In actions related to U.S. dollar LIBOR during the 
period that it was administered by the BBA, the Firm has 
obtained dismissal of certain actions and resolved certain 
other actions, and others are in various stages of litigation. 
The United States District Court for the Southern District of 
New York has granted class certification of antitrust claims 
related to bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by the 
defendants, including the Firm. A consolidated putative 
class action related to the period that U.S. dollar LIBOR was 
administered by ICE Benchmark Administration has been 
dismissed. In addition, a group of individual plaintiffs filed a 
lawsuit asserting antitrust claims, alleging that the Firm and 
other defendants were engaged in an unlawful agreement 
to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and conspired to monopolize the 
market for LIBOR-based consumer loans and credit cards. 
Defendants moved to dismiss plaintiffs’ complaint. In 
December 2021, the court denied plaintiffs’ motions for a 
preliminary injunction seeking to enjoin defendants from 
setting U.S. dollar LIBOR and enforcing any financial 
instruments that rely on U.S. dollar LIBOR. The Firm’s 
settlements of putative class actions related to Swiss franc 
LIBOR, the Singapore Interbank Offered Rate and the 
Singapore Swap Offer Rate, and the Australian Bank Bill 
Swap Reference Rate remain subject to court approval.

former officers and directors of the Firm.  The complaint

175damages, disgorgement and corporate governance reforms

title: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation.
heading: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation.
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Prime, Inc., and J.P. Morgan Strategic Securities Lending Corp. are named as defendants in a putative class action filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York.
summary:
- Addresses claims seeking damages, disgorgement, and governance reforms tied to alleged supervisory failures over historical spoofing-related conduct previously resolved with the DOJ, CFTC, and SEC in September 2020, and separate fiduciary activity issues resolved with the OCC in November 2020.
- Describes the Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation in SDNY naming several JPMorgan entities, alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading for securities lending; the motion to dismiss was denied, and plaintiffs’ motion for class certification is pending and opposed.
- Notes JPMorgan Chase and subsidiaries are involved in numerous additional legal proceedings and intend to defend vigorously.
- Explains litigation reserve practices: reserves established for several hundred matters; accrual under U.S. GAAP when loss is probable and reasonably estimable; reserves reviewed and adjusted quarterly with counsel input.
- Reports legal expenses: $73 million (Q2 2022) vs. $185 million (Q2 2021); $192 million (H1 2022) vs. $213 million (H1 2021).
- Cautions that outcomes are difficult to predict, particularly with large or indeterminate damages, novel legal theories, many parties, or early-stage matters; reserves may need future adjustments.
- States the Firm currently believes, considering reserves and estimated loss ranges, that other pending legal proceedings should not have a material adverse effect on consolidated financial condition, but outcomes could exceed reserves, carry reputational consequences, and be material to results in a particular period depending on loss size and earnings.
text:
Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation . JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Prime, 
Inc., and J.P. Morgan Strategic Securities Lending Corp. are 
named as defendants in a putative class action filed in the 
United States District Court for the Southern District of New 
York. The complaint asserts violations of federal antitrust 
law and New York State common law in connection with an 
alleged conspiracy to prevent the emergence of anonymous 
exchange trading for securities lending transactions. 
Defendants’ motion to dismiss the complaint was denied. 
Plaintiffs have moved to certify a class in this action, which 
defendants are opposing.
*     *     *
In addition to the various legal proceedings discussed 
above, JPMorgan Chase and its subsidiaries are named as 
defendants or are otherwise involved in a substantial 
number of other legal proceedings. The Firm believes it has 
meritorious defenses to the claims asserted against it in its 
currently outstanding legal proceedings and it intends to 
defend itself vigorously. Additional legal proceedings may 
be initiated from time to time in the future.
The Firm has established reserves for several hundred of its 
currently outstanding legal proceedings. In accordance with 
the provisions of U.S. GAAP for contingencies, the Firm 
accrues for a litigation-related liability when it is probable 
that such a liability has been incurred and the amount of 
the loss can be reasonably estimated. The Firm evaluates its 
outstanding legal proceedings each quarter to assess its 
litigation reserves, and makes adjustments in such reserves, 
upward or downward, as appropriate, based on 
management’s best judgment after consultation with 
counsel. The Firm’s legal expense was $73 million  and 
$185 million  for the three months ended June 30, 2022 
and 2021 , respectively, and $192 million  and $213 million  
for the six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , 
respectively. There is no assurance that the Firm’s litigation 
reserves will not need to be adjusted in the future. 
In view of the inherent difficulty of predicting the outcome 
of legal proceedings, particularly where the claimants seek 
very large or indeterminate damages, or where the matters 
present novel legal theories, involve a large number of 
parties or are in early stages of discovery, the Firm cannot 
state with confidence what will be the eventual outcomes of 
the currently pending matters, the timing of their ultimate 
resolution or the eventual losses, fines, penalties or 
consequences related to those matters. JPMorgan Chase 
believes, based upon its current knowledge and after 
consultation with counsel, consideration of the material 
legal proceedings described above and after taking into account its current litigation reserves and its estimated 
aggregate range of possible losses, that the other legal 
proceedings currently pending against it should not have a 
material adverse effect on the Firm’s consolidated financial 
condition. The Firm notes, however, that in light of the 
uncertainties involved in such proceedings, there is no 
assurance that the ultimate resolution of these matters will 
not significantly exceed the reserves it has currently 
accrued or that a matter will not have material reputational 
consequences. As a result, the outcome of a particular 
matter may be material to JPMorgan Chase’s operating 
results for a particular period, depending on, among other 
factors, the size of the loss or liability imposed and the level 
of JPMorgan Chase’s income for that period.

title: Business segments - Introduction
heading: Note 25 – Business segments
start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
summary:
Business segments
The Firm is managed on an LOB basis. There are four major 
reportable business segments - Consumer & Community 
Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial 
Banking and Asset & Wealth Management. In addition, there 
is a Corporate segment. The business segments are 
determined based on the products and services provided, or 
the type of customer served, and they reflect the manner in 
which financial information is currently evaluated by the 
Firm’s Operating Committee. Segment results are presented 
on a managed basis. Refer to Segment results below, and 
Note 32 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021 Form 10-K for a further 
discussion of JPMorgan Chase ’s business segments.

title: Segment results
heading: Segment results
start_phrase: The following table provides a summary of the Firm’s segment results as of or for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , on a managed basis.
summary:
- Overview of business segmentation: The firm is managed by lines of business (LOBs) with four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance.

- Managed basis presentation: Segment results are shown on a managed, fully tax-equivalent (FTE) basis. Revenue from tax-advantaged investments and tax‑exempt securities is grossed up for comparability with taxable items; corresponding tax effects are recorded in income tax expense. Reconciling items remove these FTE adjustments to arrive at reported U.S. GAAP results.

- Capital allocation: Equity capital is assigned to each LOB; methodologies and assumptions are periodically reassessed, which can change LOB capital.

- Change in tax allocation: In 1Q22 the firm changed its methodology for allocating income taxes to LOBs; prior periods were revised for comparability with no impact on firmwide net income.

- Segment performance highlights (three months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021):
  - Firmwide: Total net revenue was approximately flat (30.7bn vs. 30.5bn). Provision for credit losses swung to a 1.1bn expense from a 2.3bn release. Noninterest expense rose to 18.7bn from 17.7bn. Net income declined to 8.65bn from 11.95bn. ROE fell to 13% from 18%; overhead ratio increased to 61 from 58.
  - CCB: Total net revenue essentially flat (12.6bn vs. 12.8bn) with higher net interest income and lower noninterest revenue; provision moved to a 761mm expense from a 1.87bn release; expenses increased. Net income fell to 3.10bn from 5.65bn; ROE 24% vs. 44%.
  - CIB: Revenue decreased (11.95bn vs. 13.21bn); slight provision expense vs. a prior release; higher expenses. Net income declined to 3.73bn from 5.02bn; ROE 14% vs. 23%. Average equity rose significantly (103bn vs. 83bn).
  - CB: Revenue increased (2.68bn vs. 2.48bn); provision expense vs. prior release; expenses up. Net income declined to 994mm from 1.42bn; ROE 15% vs. 23%.
  - AWM: Revenue increased (4.31bn vs. 4.11bn); modest provision expense vs. prior release; expenses up. Net income declined to 1.00bn from 1.16bn; ROE 23% vs. 32%.
  - Corporate: Revenue improved (80mm vs. -1.17bn). Net loss narrowed (-174mm vs. -1.30bn). Total assets rose to 1.46tn from 1.38tn.

- Balance sheet and efficiency metrics: Average equity increased notably in CIB and AWM; total assets grew across major segments. Overhead ratios rose in all operating segments, indicating higher expense-to-revenue levels.

- Reconciliation to GAAP: Segment-level FTE adjustments are eliminated in reconciling items; the Corporate reconciling column shows offsetting tax effects to align managed results with reported GAAP. References are made to the firm’s 2021 Form 10‑K (Note 32 and page 93) for additional details on segment definitions, managed basis, and capital allocation.

Segment results
The following table provides a summary of the Firm’s 
segment results as of or for the three and six months ended  
June 30, 2022 and 2021 , on a managed basis. The Firm’s 
definition of managed basis starts with the reported U.S. 
GAAP results and includes certain reclassifications to 
present total net revenue for the Firm (and each of the reportable business segments) on an FTE basis. 
Accordingly, revenue from investments that receive tax 
credits and tax-exempt securities is presented in the 
managed results on a basis comparable to taxable 
investments and securities. Refer to Note 32 of JPMorgan 
Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for additional information on the 
Firm’s managed basis.

title: Capital allocation
heading: Capital allocation
start_phrase: The amount of capital assigned to each business segment is referred to as equity.
summary:
- Defines JPMorgan Chase’s reportable business segments and management structure: operations are managed by line of business with four major segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment.
- Explains reporting on a “managed basis,” which adjusts reported U.S. GAAP results to a tax-equivalent (FTE) basis so tax-advantaged income is comparable to taxable income; corresponding tax effects are reflected in income tax expense and eliminated in reconciling items to arrive at GAAP.
- Describes capital allocation: each segment is assigned equity; assumptions and methodologies are periodically reassessed; references to the 2021 Form 10-K for further detail.
- Presents detailed segment results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, including by LOB and Corporate, plus reconciling items and Firm totals. Metrics shown: noninterest revenue, net interest income, total net revenue, provision for credit losses, noninterest expense, income before income tax, income tax expense/benefit, net income, average equity, total assets, return on equity (ROE), and overhead ratio.
- Highlights at the Firm level:
  - Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021: total net revenue roughly flat (~$30.7B vs ~$30.5B); net income down (~$8.6B vs ~$11.9B); ROE 13% vs 18%; overhead ratio 61 vs 58; credit costs shifted to a net build (~$1.1B) from a net release (~$2.3B).
  - 1H 2022 vs 1H 2021: total net revenue slightly lower (~$61.4B vs ~$62.7B); net income down (~$16.9B vs ~$26.2B); ROE 13% vs 21%; credit costs moved to a net build (~$2.6B) from a large net release (~$6.4B).
- Notes notable segment trends:
  - CCB: revenue approximately flat year over year in Q2; higher provision for credit losses and higher expenses; strong ROE though below prior year.
  - CIB: lower noninterest revenue in Q2 driving lower total revenue; expenses up; ROE decreased versus prior year.
  - CB: revenue up with higher net interest income; provision swung from release to build; ROE moderated.
  - AWM: modest revenue growth with higher expenses; ROE decreased vs prior year.
  - Corporate: small revenue and loss figures; included for reconciliation purposes.
- Provides average equity by segment (e.g., CIB average equity higher in 2022 vs 2021) and total assets by segment and Firm totals as of June 30, 2022 vs 2021.
- Footnotes disclose:
  - In Q1 2022, the Firm changed its methodology for allocating income taxes to LOBs with no impact to firmwide net income; prior periods revised.
  - Managed/FTE adjustments are eliminated in reconciling items to align with reported U.S. GAAP.
- Cross-references to Note 32 of the 2021 Form 10-K and LOB equity discussion (page 93) for additional context on segment definitions, managed basis, and capital allocation.

start_phrase:

sheet of JPMorgan Chase & Co. and its subsidiaries (the 
“Firm”) as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and the related consolidated 
statements of income, comprehensive income and changes 
in stockholders’ equity for the three-month and six-month 
periods ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 and the

summary:
- Independent review report by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP on JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s interim consolidated financial statements as of June 30, 2022, and for the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Conclusion: no material modifications are needed for the interim financial statements to conform with U.S. GAAP.
- Reference to prior audit: PwC audited the year ended December 31, 2021, issued an unqualified opinion (Feb 22, 2022), and noted a 2020 change in accounting for credit losses; the Dec 31, 2021 balance sheet information presented herein is fairly stated in relation to the audited statements.
- Basis and scope: review performed under PCAOB standards; PwC is independent under SEC and PCAOB rules; a review is primarily analytical procedures and inquiries and is substantially less in scope than an audit; no audit opinion expressed.
- Report dated August 3, 2022.

- Unaudited consolidated average balance sheets with taxable-equivalent interest and rates for Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021:
  - Total interest-earning assets: $3.386T avg in Q2’22 (yield 2.22%) vs $3.177T (1.79%).
  - Net interest income and net yield: $15,231 million, NIM 1.80% in Q2’22 vs $12,850 million, NIM 1.62% in Q2’21.
  - Interest rate spread: 1.68% in Q2’22 vs 1.57% in Q2’21.
  - Loans: $1.093T avg, yield 4.28% in Q2’22 vs $1.025T, 3.98% in Q2’21.
  - Investment securities: $672.8B avg, rate 1.55% in Q2’22 vs $585.1B, 1.31% in Q2’21; taxable vs nontaxable components shown.
  - Deposits with banks: rate rose to 0.62% from 0.06%; federal funds/reverse repos and securities borrowed show higher/lower yields with noted negative yield effects in 2021 for securities borrowed.
  - Total interest-bearing liabilities: $2.606T avg, cost 0.54% in Q2’22 vs $2.487T, 0.22% in Q2’21; higher costs across deposits, repos, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, and long-term debt (2.54% vs 1.70%).
  - Total assets: $3.912T vs $3.729T; total liabilities: $3.631T vs $3.445T.
  - Stockholders’ equity: $280.8B in Q2’22 vs $283.5B in Q2’21; preferred $32.8B; common $248.0B.
  - Noninterest-bearing deposits: $741.9B vs $654.4B.

- Footnotes highlight: tax-exempt securities treatment; inclusion of hedging derivatives in interest; amortized-cost-based securities yields; negative interest effects on securities borrowed and prime brokerage payables; short-term borrowings include commercial paper; brokerage-related customer payables classified as interest-bearing liabilities; combined trading liabilities balances disclosed.

sheet of JPMorgan Chase & Co. and its subsidiaries (the 
“Firm”) as of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2, and the related consolidated 
statements of income, comprehensive income and changes 
in stockholders’ equity for the three-month and six-month

consolidated statements of cash flows for the six-month 
periods ended J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021 , including the 
related notes (collectively referred to as the “interim 
financial statements”). Based on our reviews, we are not 
aware of any material modifications that should be made to 
the accompanying interim financial statements for them to 
be in conformity with accounting principles generally 
accepted in the United States of America.
We have previously audited, in accordance with the 
standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight 
Board (United States), the consolidated balance sheet of 
the Firm as of D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, and the related 
consolidated statements of income, comprehensive income, 
changes in stockholders’ equity and of cash flows for the 
year then ended (not presented herein), and in our report 
dated February 22, 2022, which included a paragraph 
describing a change in the manner of accounting for credit 
losses on certain financial instruments in 2020, we 
expressed an unqualified opinion on those consolidated 
financial statements. In our opinion, the information set 
forth in the accompanying consolidated balance sheet 
information as of D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, is fairly stated, in all 
material respects, in relation to the consolidated balance 
sheet from which it has been derived.  Basis for Review Results
These interim financial statements are the responsibility of 
the Firm’s management. We are a public accounting firm 
registered with the Public Company Accounting Oversight 
Board (United States) (PCAOB) and are required to be 
independent with respect to the Firm in accordance with 
the U.S. federal securities laws and the applicable rules and 
regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission and 
the PCAOB. We conducted our review in accordance with 
the standards of the PCAOB. A review of interim financial 
information consists principally of applying analytical 
procedures and making inquiries of persons responsible for 
financial and accounting matters. It is substantially less in 
scope than an audit conducted in accordance with the 
standards of the PCAOB, the objective of which is the 
expression of an opinion regarding the financial statements 
taken as a whole. Accordingly, we do not express such an 
opinion.

  - Assets: deposits with banks; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; trading assets (debt instruments); taxable and nontaxable investment securities; loans; other interest‑earning assets
